Continuous paddy residue retention builds soil organic carbon and improves nitrogen mineralization, so less external nitrogen is needed. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: My soil organic carbon is high after years of paddy residue retention. Should I reduce DAP too?
output: Yes — if continuous paddy straw retention or incorporation has raised your soil organic carbon to the high category, drill only 27 kg DAP per acre at sowing instead of the standard 55 kg DAP. This is along with the 20 kg urea reduction from the 4th year onwards on Happy Seeder wheat. The savings come from improved soil biological activity. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: What is PAU Leaf Colour Charfor wheat?
output: PAU-LCC is a colour-matching chart that helps farmers apply only the nitrogen the wheat actually needs, rather than fixed doses. About 50-55 days after sowing (before second irrigation), match the colour of the topmost fully exposed intact leaf of 10 representative plants with the chart under the shade of your body. Apply urea based on the leaf greenness reading. This achieves potential yield with optimum nitrogen, avoiding waste. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: How do I use PAU-LCC to decide urea dose at second irrigation?
output: Match leaf colour of 10 plants under your body's shade. Apply urea based on the colour reading of 6 or more out of 10 leaves: more than LCC shade 5.0 → 15 kg urea/acre; LCC shade 4.5-5.0 → 30 kg/acre; LCC shade 4.0-4.5 → 40 kg/acre; less than LCC shade 4.0 → 55 kg/acre. Greener leaves need less urea; paler leaves need more. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: My wheat leaves are very dark green. Should I still apply 45 kg urea at second irrigation?
output: No — if 6 or more out of 10 leaves match more than LCC shade 5.0 (very dark green), apply only 15 kg urea per acre at second irrigation. The dark colour indicates the crop has enough nitrogen, and adding the standard 45 kg/acre would waste fertilizer and increase lodging risk. Use PAU-LCC to match dose to actual need. Source: PAU Package es Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: My wheat leaves look pale (less than LCC shade 4.0). What urea dose at second irrigation?
output: If 6 or more out of 10 leaves match less than LCC shade 4.0 (pale yellowish green), apply 55 kg urea per acre at second irrigation — more than the standard 45 kg/acre recommendation. The pale colour signals nitrogen deficiency and the higher dose corrects it before reproductive growth peaks. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: Does PAU-LCC work for Happy Seeder sown wheat too?
output: Yes — PAU-LCC is highly beneficial for achieving potential yield with optimum fertilizer nitrogen application in both conventionally sown wheat AND wheat sown with different rice straw management options (Happy Seeder, Super Seeder, e. The leaf-colour reading reflects actual crop nitrogen status regardless of sowing method. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: What is the Green Seeker optical sensor for wheat?
output: Green Seeker is an optical sensor that reads crop greenness electronically, allowing precise nitrogen recommendations. To use it, establish an over-fertilizer nitrogen reference plot of at least 30 sq metre with the same variety and sowing date, applying 55 kg DAP + 45 kg urea per acre at sowing and 65 kg urea per acre at first irrigation. The sensor compares the main field to this reference to compute the optimal top-up urea dose. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: How do I set up a Green Seeker reference plot for wheat?
output: Establish a reference plot of at least 30 sq metres in the same field, with the same wheat variety and same sowing date as the main crop. Fertilize the reference at over-fertilizer rates: 55 kg DAP + 45 kg urea per acre at sowing, plus 65 kg urea per acre at first irrigation. The Green Seeker sensor compares your main field's reflectance to this well-fed reference to recommend a top-up urea dose. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: What are PAU's key fertilizer principles for wheat?
output: Six principles: (1) Use integrated nutrient management — combine organic, biological, and chemical fertilizers. (2) Apply 90 kg urea and 55 kg DAP per acre in medium fertility soils. (3) Apply potassium only to deficient soils. (4) Use PAU-LCC or Green Seek for need-based urea application. (5) Correct manganese, zinc, and sulphur deficiency in deficient soils. (6) To mitigate high-temperature stress at grain filling, spray potassium nitrate or salicylic acid as recommended. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: What can I spray on my wheat to protect it from heat at grain filling?
output: PAU recommends spraying potassium nitrate or salicylic acid (as per recommendation) to mitigate the effect of high temperature at the grain filling stage. This is critical in Punjab where March-April heat waves above 28°C accelerate ripening and shrink grain weight. The sprays help maintain grain fill and protect yield. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: Why does PAU say I should correct manganese, zinc, and sulphur deficiencies?
output: Punjab soils — partiarly alkaline ones — frequently show manganese, zinc, and/or sulphur deficiency, which limits wheat yield even when N, P, K are adequate. Correct these deficiencies in deficient soils based on soil tests. Zinc deficiency is especially common in alkaline Punjab soils; sulphur deficiency is increasingly common in low-organic-carbon fields. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: How do I use Green Seeker on my wheat field at second irrigation?
output: About 50-55 days after sowing (just before 2nd irrigation), record Green Seeker readings by holding the sensor 75 cm above the crop canopy. Take readings on both your test field and the over-fertilized reference plot. Feed both readings plus the crop age into the 'PAU-Urea Guide' app to get the exact urea dose to apply. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: What height should I hold the Green Seeker above my wheat?
output: Hold the Green Seeker optical sensor 75 cm above the crop canopy when taking readings — same height for the test field and the over-fertilized reference plot. Take the readings about 50-55 days after sowing, just before second irrigation. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: What is the PAU-Urea Guide app?
output: PAU-Urea Guide is a mobile app that takes Green Seeker readings (from your test field and over-fertilized reference plot) plus crop age and outputs the exact urea dose to apply. It removes guesswork from need-based nitrogen management for wheat sown by any method. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: Should I still apply urea at 55 days after sowing if the second irrigation is delayed by rain?
output: Yes — PAU emphasizes that PAU-LCC or Green Seeker based nitrogen application should be done at 55 days after sowing even if second irrigation is delayed due to rainfall. The wheat's nitrogen demand peaks at this stage regardless of irrigation timing. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: What urea solution should I spray if my wheat leaves are dark een and water is stagnating?
output: If leaf greenness is equal to or darker than PAU-LCC shade 5.5 and water is stagnating (so soil broadcast is not safe), spray 7.5% urea solution: 15 kg urea in 200 litres of water per acre. Apply two criss-cross sprays — one at 42 days after sowing and another at 54 days after sowing. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: What urea solution should I spray if my wheat leaves are pale and water is stagnating?
output: If leaf greenness is less than PAU-LCC shade 5.5 (paler) and water is stagnating, spray a stronger 10% urea solution: 20 kg urea in 20litres of water per acre. Apply two criss-cross sprays — at 42 days after sowing and at 54 days after sowing. The stronger solution corrects nitrogen deficiency that would otherwise be fixed by soil broadcast. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: What conditions must be met before using PAU-LCC or Green Seeker?
output: For PAU-LCC and Green Seeker to give accurate nitrogen recommendations, the wheat field must be free from disease/insect attack and deficiency of other nutrients (zinc, sulphur, manganese, etc.). Other stresses also dull leaf colour and confuse the readings. Aress those issues first, then use the chart or sensor for nitrogen guidance. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: Where can I buy a PAU-LCC?
output: PAU-LCC is available at the PAU Ludhiana Book Sale Counter at Gate No. 1, and at Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) and Farm Advisory Service Centres in different districts of Punjab. The chart is inexpensive and pays for itself many times over through better-targeted urea application. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: I'm sowing wheat in kallar (alkaline) soil. Should I adjust the fertilizer?
output: Yes — for wheat sown in kallar (alkaline) soil, apply 25% MORE nitrogen than the standard recommendation. Alkaline soils tie up nitrogen and limit availability, so the higher dose compensates. Standard rate is 50 kg N/acre on medium fertile soils, so kallar soil needs about 62-63 kg N/acre. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: I sowed wheat after mid-December. Should I apply less or more nitrogen?
output: Apply 25% LESS nitrogen than the standard recommendation for wheat sown after mid-December. The shorter growing seas and reduced yield potential of late-sown wheat mean lower total nitrogen demand. Standard rate is 50 kg N/acre, so late-sown wheat needs about 37-38 kg N/acre. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: I already applied the full urea dose but my wheat still looks nitrogen-deficient. What can I do?
output: Spray a 3% urea solution as a corrective foliar dose: 9 kg urea dissolved in 300 litres of water per acre. Spray cross-wise to thoroughly cover the crop. Foliar urea is rapidly absorbed through the leaves and corrects deficiency faster than another soil broadcast at this stage. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: How do I prepare a 3% corrective urea spray for wheat?
output: Dissolve 9 kg urea in 300 litres of water per acre — that's a 3% solution. Spray cross-wise (in two perpendicular passes) to thoroughly cover the crop foliage. Use this when symptoms of nitrogen deficiency persist after the full soil dose has been applied. Foliar uptake corrects deficiency within days. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: Why does PAU say to apply phosphorus to wheat and skip it on the following kharif crop?
output: Wheat is more responsive to phosphorus application than kharif crops like rice and cotton. So apply the full phosphorus dose to wheat and omit phosphorus on the following kharif crop. The residual phosphorus from the wheat application carries over and meets the kharif crop'sower phosphorus demand, saving fertilizer cost. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: Should I apply phosphorus to my rice crop after wheat?
output: No — PAU recommends omitting phosphorus on the kharif crop (rice or cotton) when full phosphorus has been applied to the preceding wheat crop. Wheat is more phosphorus-responsive than kharif crops, and the residual phosphorus carries over adequately. This saves fertilizer cost without yield penalty. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: What's a kallar soil?
output: Kallar is a Punjabi term for alkaline soils — high pH, often with soty and salinity issues. These soils tie up nitrogen and reduce its availability to crops. PAU recommends applying 25% MORE nitrogen than standard to wheat grown in kallar soil. Highly deteriorated alkaline (kallar) soils should be avoided for wheat unless amended (gypsum is the typical amendment). Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: Compare PAU-LCC and Green Seeker. Which is better?
output: Both serve the same need-based nitrogen function. PAU-LCC is a low-cost colour-matching chart, used by holding 10 wheat leaves under your body's shade and matching colour around 50-55 days after sowing. Green Seeker is a higher-cost optical sensor used 75 cm above the canopy, paired with the PAU-Urea Guide app. PAU-LCC is more accessible for smallholder farmers; Green Seeker is more precise and useful at larger scale. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: If my wheat is in good health, which fertilizer adjustment matters most?
output: Need-based nitrogen via PAU-LCC or Green Seeker is the highest-impact adjustment. Standard recommendations apply 90 kg urea/acre across the season; need-based methods can reduce this to 30-55 kg/acre at second irrigation depending on crop greenness, saving cost without yield loss. Apply this only when the field is otherwise healthy (no disease, no other nutrient deficiency). Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: When can a PAU-LCC reading SAVE me urea cost?
output: When PAU-LCC reads more than shade 5.0 (very dark green leaves), apply only 15 kg urea per acre at second irrigation — saving 30 kg urea per acre versus the standard 45 kg recommendation. The savingsome from matching dose to actual crop need, avoiding waste when the wheat already has adequate nitrogen. The chart pays for itself in one season. Source: PAU Package of Practices Rabi 2025-26.

instruction: How much rice does Punjab grow each year?
output: Rice occupied 32.43 lakh hectares in Punjab during 2024-25, producing 216.31 lakh tonnes of paddy (equivalent to 144.19 lakh tonnes of rice). Average paddy yield was 66.70 quintals per hectare (27.0 quintals per acre). Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why does PAU recommend avoiding Pusa 44, Peeli Pusa, and Dogar Pusa rice varieties?
output: PAU specifically recommends avoiding cultivation of Pusa 44, Peeli Pusa, and Dogar Pusa because they require 15-20% more water than recommended varieties and demand at least two extra pesticide sprays. Both factors lower net profit while worsening Punjab's groundwater crisis. Switch to PAU-recommended short-duration varieties for water savings and easier paddy straw management. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why should I switch to short-duration rice varieties?
output: PAU recommends short-duration rice varieties for two key reasons: water savings (less time in flooded field) and easier paddy straw management. Short-duration varieties also harvest earlier, leaving more time for clean transition to wheat without burning straw. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I sow rice nursery and transplant rice in Punjab?
output: Sow rice nursery between 20 May and 20 June, and transplant between 20 June and 10 July. This timely schedule gives better grain quality, saves water, and reduces stem borer build-up. Earlier transplanting violates the Punjab Subsoil Water Preservation Act and accelerates groundwater depletion. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I want to grow PR 126 rice. What nursery age should I transplant?
output: For higher yield and better grain quality from PR 126, transplant 25-30 day old nursery. Older or younger nursery seedlings reduce yield and quality. Stay within the timely transplanting window of 20 June to 10 July. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is direct seeded rice in tar-wattar field?
output: Direct Seeded Rice (DSR) in tar-wattar (moist) field is sown directly into a moist seedbed from 1 June onwards, skipping puddling and transplanting. PAU recommends DSR for higher savings in irrigation water — typically 15-20% less water than puddled transplanted rice. It also reduces labour costs and shortens the field-occupation period. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I apply phosphorus to my rice if I already gave full P to the previous wheat?
output: No — PAU explicitly recommends omitting phosphorus application in rice following wheat that received the recommended dose of phosphatic fertilizer. Wheat is more phosphorus-responsive than rice, and the residual phosphorus from the wheat application carries over adequatto meet rice's lower demand. This saves fertilizer cost. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How should I decide rice nitrogen dose?
output: Apply nitrogen on the basis of soil test, and use it judiciously based on the Leaf Colour Chart (LCC). Excessive nitrogen application encourages multiplication of insect pests (especially planthoppers) and increases disease incidence. PAU's LCC-guided approach matches dose to actual crop need and protects both yield and pest profile. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What's the danger of applying too much nitrogen to rice?
output: Excessive nitrogen application encourages multiplication of insect pests (especially planthoppers) and diseases. The dense, lush canopy from over-fertilization is more attractive to pests, and weakened plant tissues are more disease-prone. Use Leaf Colour Chart (LCC) to apply only what the crop needs, and base your dose on a soil test. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I plant PR 131 rice in sub-mountainous Punjab?
output: No — PAU specifically advises avoiding planting of PR 131 in sub-mountainous areas. The variety is recommended for other regions oPunjab but performs poorly in sub-mountainous microclimates. Choose a different recommended variety for those areas. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I am growing PR 132 rice. How does my fertilizer need differ?
output: For higher yield from PR 132, apply 25% LESS nitrogenous fertilizer than the rate used for other varieties. PR 132 is more nitrogen-efficient and over-application would actually reduce yield while increasing pest pressure. Soil test plus LCC-guided splits remain the precise approach. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I start fungicide spray for false smut in rice?
output: Initiate spray of recommended fungicides at the boot stage of the rice crop to control false smut disease. Spraying earlier is wasted; spraying later misses the protective window because boot stage is when developing panicles are most vulnerable to infection. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I use synthetic pyrethroids on my rice crop?
output: No — PAU explicitly says synthetic pyrethroids should NOT be used for control of rice insect-pests. Pyrethroids increase the population of rice planthoppers (resurgence effect) by killing the planthoppers' natural predators while sparing the planthoppers themselves. Use the specifically recommended planthopper insecticides instead. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I stop irrigating my rice before harvest?
output: Stop irrigation about a fortnight (15 days) before maturity. Continued irrigation near maturity delays harvest, reduces grain quality, complicates straw management, and wastes water. Stopping at the right time also lets the field firm up enough for combine harvest. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I harvest my rice?
output: Harvest at proper maturity, and follow variety-specific timing — different varieties mature on different schedules. Avoid harvesting at night because dew makes the grain wet, reducing storage quality and increasing breakage during threshing. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What climatic conditions does rice need in Punjab?
output: Rice prefers high temperature, high humidity, prolonged sunshine, and assured water supply. For high productivity in Punjab, maximum temperature should remain within 34-40°C (vegetative), 33-35°C (flowering), 32-35°C (grain development); minimum within 23-28°C, 25-27°C, 20-25°C respectively; and bright sunshine 7-11, 6-10, 7-10 hours/day during these stages. Source: PAU Package of Pracarif 2025.

instruction: Can I grow rice on my soil with high pH?
output: Yes — rice tolerates a wide range of soil reactions from pH 5 to 9. Rice grows well on soils with low permeability (which traps the standing water rice prefers). Loamy soils are the best for rice cultivation. Note that severely alkaline (kallar) or saline soils may still need amendment for reliable yields. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Tell me about PR 133 rice variety.
output: PR 133 (2026) is a high-yielding medium-duration rice variety. It matures in about 111 days after transplanting, plant height around 109 cm, and is resistant to all ten races of the major rice diseases. As a 2026 release, it is the latest PAU recommendation for Punjab cultivation. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What are planthoppers and why are they dangerous?
output: Planthoppers (whitebacked and brown) feed at the base of rice plants and are often overlooked because the damage is hidden low in the canopy. Damage is only noticed when the crop becomes hopper-burnt — at which point yield loss is severe. Regular monitoring of insect populations is essential. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is PR 133 rice and how is it different from older varieties?
output: PR 133 (2026) is the latest PAU rice variety, high-yielding and medium-duration. It matures in about 111 days after transplanting, plant height 109 cm, paddy yield 30.5 quintals per acre. Crucially, it is resistant to all ten pathotypes of bacterial blight currently prevalent in Punjab. Long slender translucent grains with high total and head rice recoveries. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Tell me about PR 132 rice variety.
output: PR 132 (2025) is a high-yielding, medium-duration, nitrogen-use-efficient variety. It performs best at 75 percent of the recommended nitrogen dose (25 percent lower than other varieties). Higher nitrogen risks lodging. Plant height 113 cm, matures in 111 days after transplanting, yields 31.5 quintals per acre. Resistant to 6 of the 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes in Punjab. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why is PR 132 nitrogen-efficient and how should I fertilize it?
output: PR 132 is bred for nitrogen-use efficiency and performs best at 75 percent of the recommended nitrogen dose. Apply 25 percent less nitrogenous fertilizer than other varieties. Going higher poses lodging risk because the variety produces excess vegetative growth. Even at the reduced rate, expect 31.5 quintals per acre. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Which PAU rice variety has the highest yield?
output: Among recently released medium-duration varieties, PR 132 (2025) leads at 31.5 quintals per acre, followed by PR 131 (2022) at 31.0 quintals per acre. Both are recommended for timely transplanting. PR 132 has the bonus of nitrogen-use efficiency (apply 25 percent less N), while PR 131 is fully resistant to all 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes in Punjab. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I want a rice variety that resists lodging. Which should I pick?
output: PAU specifically labels PR 131 (2022) and PR 130 (2022) as lodging-tolerant. PR 131 yields 31.0 quintals per acre and matures in 110 days; PR 130 yields 30.0 quintals per acre and matures earlier in 105 days. Both are resistant to all 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes. Avoid HKR 47 if lodging is a concern as it is prone to lodging. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What's the shortest-duration PAU rice variety with full bacterial blight resistance?
output: PR 130 (2022) at 105 days after transplanting is the shortest-duration variety with full resistance to all 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes in Punjab. Plant height 108 cm, yields 30.0 quintals per acre. It is also lodging-tolerant. The short cycle helps water savings and quicker turnover to wheat. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Tell me about PR 130 rice.
output: PR 130 (2022) is a high-yielding, mid-early, lodging-tolerant rice variety. Plant height 108 cm, matures in 105 days after transplanting, yields 30.0 quintals per acre. Long slender translucent and lustrous grains with high total and head rice recoveries. Resistant to all 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes in Punjab. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is PR 129 rice?
output: PR 129 (2020) is an improved version of the older PAU 201. Long slender clear translucent grains. Plant height 105 cm, matures in 108 days after transplanting, yields 30.0 quintals per acre. Resistant to all 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes in Punjab. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the difference between PR 128 and PR 129?
output: Both PR 128 (2020) and PR 129 (2020) are improved versions of PAU 201, both with long slender clear translucent grains and resistance to all 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes. Differences: PR 128 plant height 110 cm, matures in 111 days, yields 30.5 quintals per acre. PR 129 plant height 105 cm, matures in 108 days, yields 30.0 quintals per acre. PR 129 is slightly shorter in both height and duration. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Tell me about HKR 47 rice variety.
output: HKR 47 (2020) is a mid-early maturing rice variety taking about 104 days to mature after transplanting with average plant height 117 cm. Long slender clear translucent grains, yield 29.5 quintals per acre. Important caveats: it is SUSCEPTIBLE to all 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes in Punjab and is also prone to lodging. PAU lists it but PR 130 or PR 131 are safer choices for similar duration. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I avoid HKR 47 rice?
output: Use caution with HKR 47 (2020). It yields 29.5 quintals per acre and matures in 104 days, but it is susceptible to all 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes in Punjab and prone to lodging. PR 130 (2022) is a comparable mid-early variety (105 days) with better disease resistance and lodging tolerance, yielding 30.0 quintals per acre. PR 130 is the safer choice unless you have specific reasons to grow HKR 47. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Tell me about PR 127 rice variety.
output: PR 127 (2018) is a medium-maturing rice variety. Average plant height 104 cm, matures in about 107 days after transplanting. Long slender clear translucent grains with high total and head rice recoveries. It is one of PAU's reliable medium-duration choices for Punjab cultivation. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is bacterial blight in rice and which varieties resist it?
output: Bacterial blight is a major rice disease caused by Xanthomonas oryzae. PAU tracks 10 prevalent pathotypes in Punjab. Varieties resistant to all 10 pathotypes: PR 131, PR 130, PR 129, PR 128, and PR 133 (2026). PR 132 (2025) is resistant to 6 of 10. HKR 47 is susceptible to all 10. Choose a fully-resistant variety when bacterial blight pressure is high. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What does high total and head rice recovery mean?
output: Total rice recovery is the percentage of milled rice obtained from paddy. Head rice recovery is the percentage of unbroken whole-grain rice from milling. High values for both indicate better milling quality and higher market value. PAU varieties like PR 133, PR 132, PR 131, PR 130, PR 129, PR 128 all have high total and head rice recoveries with long slender translucent grains. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I have heavy bacterial blight pressure in my area. Which rice variety should I grow?
output: Choose a variety resistant to all 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes in Punjab. PAU recommends PR 131, PR 130, PR 129, PR 128, or the newest PR 133 (2026). Avoid HKR 47 entirely (susceptible to all 10) and PR 132 (resistant to only 6 of 10). PR 131 yields highest among the fully-resistant set at 31.0 quintals per acre. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What grain quality should I expect from current PAU rice varieties?
output: Current PAU rice varieties (PR 127 onwards through PR 133) all share a desirable grain profile: long, slender, clear translucent grains with high total and head rice recoveries. PR 130 specifically has lustrous grains. These traits give better cooking quality, market acceptability, and milling yields than older varieties. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Compare PR 131 and PR 130 rice varieties.
output: Both 2022 releases, both lodging-tolerant, both resistant to all 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes. Differences: PR 131 plant height 111 cm, matures in 110 days, yields 31.0 quintals per acre, medium-maturing. PR 130 plant height 108 cm, matures in 105 days, yields 30.0 quintals per acre, mid-early. Choose PR 131 for slightly higher yield, PR 130 for shorter cycle and faster water turnover. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Which rice variety should I pick if water savings are my top priority?
output: Pick a short-duration variety to spend less time in flooded paddy. PR 130 (105 days, 30.0 q/acre, fully bacterial blight resistant) is ideal. HKR 47 is also short at 104 days but susceptible to disease. Even better, consider Direct Seeded Rice (DSR) using a recommended short-duration variety, sown in tar-wattar field from 1 June onwards for additional 15-20 percent water savings. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Tell me about PR 127 rice variety in detail.
output: PR 127 (2018) is a medium-maturing rice variety with plant height 104 cm, matures in 107 days after transplanting, yields 30.0 quintals per acre. Long slender translucent grains with high total and head rice recoveries. Resistant to all 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes in Punjab. Important caveat: do NOT grow PR 127 in alkali soils or under brackish water. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Can I grow PR 127 rice on alkali soil?
output: No — PAU specifically warns NOT to grow PR 127 in alkali soils or under brackish water. The variety performs well otherwise (30.0 quintals per acre, full bacterial blight resistance, 107 days), but alkalinity or saline irrigation severely reduces yield. For alkali-affected fields, choose a different variety after first amending the soil with gypsum. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the shortest-duration rice variety from PAU?
output: PR 126 (2017) is PAU's earliest-maturing rice variety, taking only 93 days after transplanting. Plant height 102 cm, yields 30.0 quintals per acre. Long slender clear translucent grains. Resistant to 7 of the 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes in Punjab. Use 25-30 day old nursery for best yield and grain quality. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Tell me about PR 126 rice and what nursery age to use.
output: PR 126 (2017) is an early-maturing rice variety, just 93 days after transplanting. Transplant 25-30 day old nursery for higher yield and better grain quality. Plant height 102 cm, paddy yield 30.0 quintals per acre, resistant to 7 of 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes. Long slender clear translucent grains. Best for water savings and quick rotation to wheat. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Tell me about PR 122 rice variety.
output: PR 122 (2013) is a long-duration variety maturing in 117 days after transplanting with plant height 108 cm. Long slender translucent grains, yield 31.5 quintals per acre — among the highest in PAU's recommendations. Resistant to all 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes in Punjab. The longer cycle uses more water than shorter-duration varieties. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is PR 121 rice and is it lodging tolerant?
output: PR 121 (2013) is a short-statured (98 cm), stiff-strawed, lodging-tolerant rice variety with dark green erect leaves. Matures in 110 days after transplanting, yields 30.5 quintals per acre. Long slender translucent grains with good cooking quality. Resistant to all 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes in Punjab. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I want a rice variety with the best cooking quality. Which one?
output: PR 121 (2013) is specifically noted by PAU for good cooking quality, with long slender translucent grains. It is also lodging-tolerant, stiff-strawed, with dark green erect leaves. Plant height 98 cm, matures in 110 days after transplanting, yields 30.5 quintals per acre. Resistant to all 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Tell me about PR 114 rice variety.
output: PR 114 (1999) is an older variety with narrow dark green erect leaves. Plant height 102 cm, matures in 115 days after transplanting, yields 27.5 quintals per acre — lower than newer varieties. Notable for extra long clear translucent grains, but resistant to only 5 of the 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes. Newer varieties like PR 130 or PR 131 offer better disease resistance and higher yield. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Tell me about PR 113 rice variety.
output: PR 113 (1998) is one of PAU's older varieties. Plant height 105 cm, matures in 112 days after transplanting, yields 28.0 quintals per acre. Distinctive for bold heavy grains (rather than the slender style of newer varieties). Resistant to 8 of the 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes. Newer varieties like PR 122 offer higher yield (31.5 q/acre) and full bacterial blight resistance. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why does PAU recommend against Pusa 44, Peeli Pusa, and Dogar Pusa?
output: PAU strongly recommends against these long-duration varieties for several reasons: they consume 15-20 percent more water than PR varieties, produce more straw load (worsens straw burning problem), are susceptible to all prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes in Punjab, and have severe insect/disease outbreak risk demanding at least 2 extra pesticide sprays. Net profit is lower despite higher gross yield. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why is straw load a problem with Pusa 44 type long-duration rice varieties?
output: Long-duration varieties like Pusa 44, Peeli Pusa, and Dogar Pusa produce more straw than short-duration PR varieties. More straw means more residue management burden after harvest, more difficulty incorporating with Happy Seeder or Super Seeder, and more incentive for farmers to burn straw — which contributes to north India's air pollution crisis. PAU specifically discourages these varieties for this reason. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I sow my rice nursery for conventional transplanting?
output: For conventional transplanting, the optimum nursery sowing window is 20 May to 20 June. Specific dates by variety: PR 133, PR 132, PR 131, PR 129, PR 128, PR 122, PR 121, PR 114, and PR 113 should be sown 20-25 May. PR 127, PR 130, and HKR 47 should be sown 25-31 May. PR 126 has the broadest window: 25 May to 20 June. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I sow PR 131 nursery?
output: Sow PR 131 nursery between 20 and 25 May for conventional transplanting. The same window applies to PR 133, PR 132, PR 129, PR 128, PR 122, PR 121, PR 114, and PR 113. Avoid earlier sowing — it advances rice into hotter weather and worsens water demand. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I sow PR 126 nursery?
output: PR 126 has the broadest nursery sowing window — 25 May to 20 June. This flexibility makes it ideal for farmers who couldn't start in late May. Combined with its 93-day duration after transplanting, PR 126 is the most flexible variety for late-onset rice planning. Use 25-30 day old nursery for best yield. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I sow PR 130 or HKR 47 nursery?
output: Sow PR 130 and HKR 47 nursery between 25 and 31 May. Same window applies to PR 127. This is slightly later than the 20-25 May window used for most other varieties. The differences come from each variety's specific physiology and how its development matches Punjab's monsoon and temperature curves. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Which PAU rice varieties are resistant to all 10 bacterial blight pathotypes?
output: Six varieties are fully resistant to all 10 prevalent bacterial blight pathotypes in Punjab: PR 133 (2026), PR 131 (2022), PR 130 (2022), PR 129 (2020), PR 128 (2020), PR 127 (2018), PR 122 (2013), and PR 121 (2013). Use these for high disease-pressure areas. Avoid HKR 47 (susceptible to all 10) and Pusa 44/Peeli Pusa/Dogar Pusa (susceptible). Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I have brackish irrigation water. Which rice variety should I avoid?
output: Do not grow PR 127 under brackish water or in alkali soils — PAU explicitly warns against this. PR 127 has plant height 104 cm, 107-day duration, and full bacterial blight resistance under normal conditions, but salinity damages its yield severely. For brackish-water fields, choose other recommended variies or amend the soil/water first. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Which rice variety has the highest yield among PAU recommendations?
output: Among PAU's recommended rice varieties, PR 132 (2025) and PR 122 (2013) tie at 31.5 quintals per acre, followed by PR 131 (2022) at 31.0 quintals per acre. PR 132 is nitrogen-efficient (use 25 percent less N) but resistant to only 6 of 10 bacterial blight pathotypes. PR 122 is fully resistant. PR 131 is fully resistant and lodging-tolerant. Choose based on disease pressure and nitrogen access. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I select good rice seed for transplanting?
output: Dip seed in suitable lots in water in a tub or bucket, stir, and remove immature grains floating at the top. Heavy seeds settle at the bottom. Eight kg of heavy seed is sufficient for transplanting one acre. Heavy seed ensures healthy, sturdy, and uniform seedlings. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much rice seed do I need for one acre nursery?
output: Eight kg of heavy seed is sufficient for raising rice nursery to transplant one acre. Broadcast the 8 kg of seed over 160 square metres (6.5 marlas). Always select heavy seed by water-flotation to remove immature grains and ensure uniform vigorous seedlings. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I treat rice seed before sowing?
output: Treat rice seed with Sprint 75 WS (carbendazim plus mancozeb) by making a slurry of 3 g fungicide in 10-12 mL water per kg of seed. For 8 kg of seed (one acre nursery), use 24 g fungicide in 80-100 mL water. Apply the slurry to the seed before sowing for protection against seed-borne fungal diseases. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much farmyard manure should I add to my rice nursery field?
output: Mix 12 to 15 tonnes of well-rotten farmyard manure or compost per acre into the soil before nursery sowing. This builds soil organic matter, improves moisture retention, and supplies slow-release nutrients to the seedlings. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I prepare the rice nursery field for sowing?
output: Mix 12-15 tonnes of well-rotten FYM/compost per acre into the soil. Irrigate the field to germinate weeds, then plough twice after about a week to kill the germinated weeds. This stale-seedbed approach reduces weed pressure on the rice seedlings. Then prepare for nursery sowing on flat or 1.0 m wide beds. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How long does rice seed take to sprout for nursery?
output: After treating with Sprint 75 WS fungicide slurry, spread the seed in a 7-8 cm thick layer over wet gunny bags and cover with wet gunny bags. Sprinkle water periodically to keep the seed moist. Seeds sprout in about 24 to 36 hours. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What fertilizer should I apply to my rice nursery at sowing?
output: At nursery sowing, apply 26 kg urea, 60 kg single superphosphate, and 40 kg zinc sulphate heptahydrate (21 percent Zn) or 25.5 kg zinc sulphate monohydrate (33 percent Zn) per acre. The zinc is critical because Punjab alkaline soils commonly show zinc deficiency. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I use 21 percent zinc sulphate or 33 percent zinc sulphate for rice nursery?
output: Either works at PAU-equivalent rates. Use 40 kg of zinc sulphate heptahydrate (21 percent Zn) per acre, OR 25.5 kg of zinc sulphate monohydrate (33 percent Zn) per acre. Both supply roughly the same elemental zinc. The 33 percent monohydrate form is more concentrated and saves transport, which is why it has gained popularity. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much area do I need for raising rice nursery for one acre transplanting?
output: Sow 8 kg of treated heavy seed by broadcasting over 160 square metres (6.5 marlas) of nursery area to raise enough seedlings for transplanting one acre of paddy. This works out to 50 grams of seed per square metre on the nursery bed. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I protect my rice nursery seed from birds?
output: Immediately after broadcasting rice seed in the nursery, broadcast a thin layer of well-decomposed farmyard manure over the seeds. The FYM cover hides the seed from birds while still allowing germination. Without this cover, birds can cause serious nursery losses. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I apply the second dose of urea to rice nursery?
output: Apply another 26 kg urea per acre about a fortnight (15 days) after sowing the nursery. This second dose powers the seedlings to be ready for transplanting in 25-30 days. If circumstances force you to use 45-day-old or older nursery, apply the second urea dose at 4 weeks instead. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I know when my rice seedlings are ready for transplanting?
output: Rice seedlings are ready for transplanting when they are 20-25 cm tall and have 6 to 7 leaves. Normally this occurs at 25-30 days after nursery sowing if you applied the recommended fertilizer schedule. Older nursery (45 days or more) yields less and produces weaker seedlings, so plan transplanting around the 25-30 day window. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is bed sowing for rice nursery?
output: Bed sowing for rice nursery uses 1.0 metre wide beds on medium to heavy textured soils. Broadcast seed on the beds, cover well with soil and well-decomposed FYM. PAU recommends bed sowing for vigorous and healthy nursery raising, especially on heavier soils where flat nurseries can waterlog. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I irrigate a bed-sown rice nursery?
output: Apply the first irrigation immediately after sowing on the 1 metre wide beds. Apply the second irrigation around 4-6 days later when seedlings start emerging. After the second irrigation, apply need-based irrigation depending on soil type and weather. Use the same fertilizer rates as for flat-sown nursery. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I keep water standing in my rice field continuously?
output: No — PAU recommends keeping water standing in the paddy field only for 2 weeks (the establishment period). After that, apply irrigation only 2 days after the previously ponded water has infiltrated into the soil. This is intermittent flooding rather than continuous flooding. It saves significant water without reducing yield. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I save water in my rice field after the establishment period?
output: ter 2 weeks of continuous standing water following transplanting, switch to intermittent flooding: apply irrigation 2 days AFTER the ponded water has infiltrated into the soil rather than topping up before it disappears. Combined with laser-levelled fields and short-duration varieties like PR 126 or PR 130, this approach significantly reduces water use without yield penalty. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What should I do if I see insects or disease in my rice nursery?
output: If any insect attack or disease appears in the rice nursery, adopt PAU's recommended plant protection measures specific to that pest or disease. Continue regular irrigation. Acting at the nursery stage prevents the problem from carrying into the transplanted main field, where damage is much harder to control. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I use laser land leveller before rice transplanting?
output: Yes - PAU recommends levelling the field with a laser land leveller before direct sowing or transplanting of rice. Laser levelling improves water distribution uniformity, reduces total water use, prevents puddles and dry patches, and increases yield by ensuring uniform crop establishment. It is one of PAU's specifically highlighted important hints. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the PAU tractor operated nursery seeder used for?
output: The PAU tractor operated nursery seeder can sow rice nursery for both mechanical mat-type transplanting AND manual transplanting without polythene sheet on beds. This versatility lets the same machine serve farmers using different transplanting methods. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: My rice nursery shows yellowing of new leaves. What should I spray?
output: Yellowing of new leaves indicates iron deficiency. Spray three times at weekly intervals with a 0.5 to 1 percent ferrous sulphate solution. That is 0.5 to 1.0 kg of ferrous sulphate dissolved in 100 litres of water per acre. Three weekly sprays correct the deficiency before transplanting. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: My rice nursery leaves turned yellow then rusty brown. What's wrong?
output: Yellow followed by rusty brown leaves indicates zinc deficiency, common in alkaline Punjab soils. Spray either 0.5 percent zinc sulphate heptahydrate solution (500 g in 100 litres of water per acre) OR 0.3 percent zinc sulphate monohydrate solution (300 g in 100 litres of water per acre). The pre-sowing zinc application at 40 kg/acre normally prevents this; foliar spray corrects late-stage symptoms. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I control swank weed in my rice nursery?
output: Swank and other annual grasses are the main rice nursery weeds. Three options: (1) 1200 mL per acre Butachlor 50 EC mixed with 60 kg sand applied 7 days after broadcasting seed. (2) 500 mL per acre Sofit 37.5 EC (pretilachlor with safener) as sand mix, 3 days after sowing. (3) 100 mL per acre Nominee Gold or Taarak or Wash out or Macho 10 SC (bispyribac) sprayed in 150 litres of water at 15-20 days after sowing. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When do I apply Butachlor for rice nursery weed control?
output: Apply 1200 mL per acre of Butachlor 50 EC mixed with 60 kg of sand seven days after broadcasting rice seed in the nursery. The sand-mix application gives even coverage. Butachlor controls swank and other annual grasses, the main weeds in rice nursery. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is Sofit 37.5 EC and when do I apply it to rice nursery?
output: Sofit 37.5 EC is a pretilachlor with safener readymix for rice nursery weed control. Apply 500 mL per acre as a sand mix three days after sowing rice seed. The safener protects rice seedlings from herbicide injury while killing swank and other annual grasses. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is bispyribac and when do I apply it for rice nursery?
output: Bispyribac (sold as Nominee Gold, Taarak, Wash out, or Macho 10 SC) is a post-emergence herbicide for rice nursery. Apply 100 mL per acre as a spray in 150 litres of water 15 to 20 days after sowing the nursery. Use it when grassy weeds are visible above the seedlings. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I prepare for mat-type rice nursery for mechanical transplanting?
output: Select fertile soil with assured irrigation, minimum transport distance to the main field, no stones or hard material, preferably laser-levelled, and 20 metres away from tubewell and trees. Prepare at proper moisture. Spread 50 to 60 gauge polythene sheet, 90 cm wide, with 1 to 2 mm diameter perforations. About 270 grams of polythene spread to 15 metres length covers 150 mats - enough for one acre of transplanting. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What size of compartments do I need for the rice transplanter mat frames?
output: Compartment size depends on the transplanter machine. For engine-operated transplanters use 45 by 21 by 2 cm compartments. For self-propelled transplanters use 58 by 28 by 2 cm compartments. The number and size vary by machine specifications - check your machine manual. Place iron frames over the polythene sheet, fill soil uniformly from both sides up to the top surface. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much pre-germinated seed do I put in each rice transplanter mat compartment?
output: Spread 50 to 60 grams of pre-germinated rice seed evenly in each compartment of the rice transplanter mat frame. Aim for 2 to 3 seeds per square centimetre in the mat. For uniform distribution use a drum-type nursery sowing seeder with openings of 1 cm diameter along its roller. About 10 to 12 kg of seed is sufficient to sow 150 mats for one acre of transplanting. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much rice seed do I need for one acre of mechanical transplanting?
output: About 10 to 12 kg of pre-germinated seed is sufficient to sow approximately 150 mats, which is enough for one acre of mechanical transplanting. This is more than the 8 kg used for conventional manual transplanting because mat-type seedlings are denser. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How fast can two people sow rice mat-type nursery?
output: Two persons can sow rice mat-type seedlings for 3 to 4 acres in a single day using the iron frame and polythene sheet method. After sowing each mat, lift the frames and place them at the next position to repeat the procedure. This makes mechanical transplanting practical for medium-sized farms. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why does the rice mat nursery field need to be 20 metres away from tubewell and trees?
output: PAU recommends siting the mat-type rice nursery at least 20 metres from tubewells and trees. This avoids the cooler microclimate near tubewells (which slows germination) and prevents tree roots from competing for moisture and nutrients with the dense nursery seedlings. Tree shade also creates uneven growth across the mats. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I cover and water rice transplanter mat seeds after sowing?
output: After spreading 50-60 g of pre-germinated seed in each compartment, cover seeds with a thin layer of soil. Sprinkle water with a hand sprayer for proper setting of the soil. Then irrigate the field the same day. Use gentle water flow for the first 2 to 3 irrigations to avoid washing soil and seeds out of the mats. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I use 50-gauge or 60-gauge polythene sheet for rice mat nursery?
output: Either works. PAU specifies 50 to 60 gauge polythene sheet, 90 cm wide, with 1 to 2 mm diameter perforations. The perforations allow drainage while keeping seeds in place. Total polythene weight of about 270 g (spread to 15 metres length) is enough for 150 mats per acre of mechanical transplanting. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is a drum-type nursery sowing seeder?
output: A drum-type nursery sowing seeder is a manual tool used for uniform seed distribution across rice transplanter mats. Its length matches the width of the iron frame, and it has openings of 1 cm diameter along the full length of the roller. Rolling it across the soil-filled compartments deposits seed at the target density of 2-3 seeds per square cm. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why does PAU specify no stones in the mat nursery field?
output: Stones or hard material in the soil interfere with the iron frame placement, prevent uniform soil filling of compartments, and damage the polythene sheet. They also catch on transplanter machinery later. Choose a stone-free patch of fertile soil with assured irrigation for the mat nursery, separate from your main rice field if needed. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How many rice mats do I need for one acre of mechanical transplanting?
output: About 150 mats are needed for one acre of mechanical transplanting. Each mat is sown with 50-60 g of pre-germinated seed at 2-3 seeds per sq cm, using compartments of 45x21x2 cm (engine-operated transplanter) or 58x28x2 cm (self-propelled transplanter). Total seed requirement: 10-12 kg per acre of mat nursery. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How should I irrigate rice mat nursery for the first few irrigations?
output: For the first 2-3 irrigations after sowing rice mats, the flow of water should be very mild and the level uniform so that newly formed mats are not damaged. Take care that seedling mats are always wet. Strong water flow washes seeds and soil out of compartments and ruins the mat structure. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I top-dress fertilizer on rice mat nursery?
output: Spray fertilizer after an interval of about 10 days from sowing. Dissolve 200 g of urea in 15 litres of water for spraying on 150 mats. The interval ensures the seedlings have established before the second nutrient boost. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How long does rice mat nursery take to be ready for transplanting?
output: Rice mat seedlings are ready after 25-30 days of sowing. Drain water from the nursery field a few hours before uprooting. Use a sharp blade or knife to cut along the nursery boundaries of each mat. The uprooted mats are then ready for transport to the field for mechanical transplanting. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I prepare rice mat nursery for transport?
output: Drain water from the nursery field a few hours before uprooting the mats. Then give a clean cut with a sharp blade or knife along the nursery boundaries of each mat. The uprooted seedling mats are now ready for transport to the main field for transplanting. The PAU nursery cutter can be used for this cutting step (see Annexure V in the PAU Package). Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the tractor-operated seeder for mat-type paddy nursery?
output: The tractor-operated seeder for mat-type paddy nursery is a machine that lays a 1.0 m wide perforated polythene sheet (50-60 gauge) over a 1.0 m wide soil bed AND simultaneously places seed uniformly over the soil bed in a single pass. It speeds up mat nursery preparation for mechanical paddy transplanters. The same mat-type nursery can also be used for manual transplanting. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Can I use rice mat-type nursery for manual transplanting?
output: Yes. Mat-type nursery is primarily designed for mechanical transplanters but PAU notes it can also be used for manual transplanting. The dense uniform seedling distribution gives good establishment regardless of transplanting method. The PAU tractor-operated nursery seeder also supports both modes. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much organic manure should I apply before transplanting rice?
output: Before preparatory tillage for transplanting rice, apply per acre any ONE of: 6 tonnes farmyard manure, OR 6 tonnes press mud, OR 2.5 tonnes poultry manure, OR 2.4 tonnes dried gobar gas plant slurry, OR 2.0 tonnes prali char (paddy straw biochar). All five give equivalent benefits in soil health and crop response. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is green manuring and why should I do it before rice?
output: Green manuring is growing a fast-growing legume (dhaincha, cowpea, or sunnhemp) and burying it in soil before transplanting rice. It is a practical alternative when organic manures like FYM are not available in required quantities. Green manuring saves 25 kg N per acre (55 kg urea), improves soil health, and dhaincha specifically also ameliorates iron deficiency in rice. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much dhaincha seed should I sow for green manuring?
output: Sow 20 kg per acre of dhaincha seed pre-soaked in water for 8 hours, after pre-sowing irrigation (rauni) following wheat or any other preceding crop. Sow up to the first week of May. Bury the 6-8 week old dhaincha one day before transplanting paddy. This practice saves 25 kg N per acre (55 kg urea) and ameliorates iron deficiency in rice. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much cowpea seed should I sow for green manuring before rice?
output: Sow 12 kg of cowpea seed per acre, or 20 kg per acre if using bold-seeded cowpea variety. After pre-sowing irrigation (rauni) following wheat harvest, sow up to the first week of May. Bury the 6-8 week old cowpea one day before transplanting paddy. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much sunnhemp seed do I need for green manuring before rice?
output: Sow 20 kg of sunnhemp seed per acre after pre-sowing irrigation, up to the first week of May. Bury the 6-8 week old sunnhemp one day before transplanting paddy. Sunnhemp is one of three PAU-recommended green manure crops for rice along with dhaincha and cowpea. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I apply phosphorus to my green manure crop?
output: If your soil tests low in phosphorus, apply 75 kg superphosphate per acre to the dhaincha, cowpea, or sunnhemp green manure crop. Then OMIT phosphorus application to the succeeding rice crop - the green manure decomposition releases enough phosphorus for the rice. This is more efficient than direct phosphorus application to rice. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I have kallar (alkaline) soil. Which green manure is best before rice?
output: Dhaincha should be preferred in kallar (alkaline) and recently reclaimed soils. It tolerates the soil chemistry better than cowpea or sunnhemp, and dhaincha specifically also ameliorates iron deficiency in rice (a common issue on alkaline Punjab soils). Sow 20 kg seed per acre, pre-soaked 8 hours, before the first week of May. Bury 6-8 weeks later, one day before paddy transplanting. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How long should I let green manure grow before burying it?
output: Bury dhaincha, cowpea, or sunnhemp at 6 to 8 weeks of age, one day before transplanting paddy. Younger plants have less biomass; older plants become woody and decompose more slowly. The 6-8 week window also matches the typical rice transplanting schedule of mid-June to mid-July. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I grew moong before rice. How much should I reduce nitrogen?
output: If the moong crop has been incorporated into the soil one day before transplanting paddy (after pod picking), reduce the fertilizer nitrogen dose for rice by one-third. The moong residue's biological nitrogen contribution and decomposition supply enough N to offset the reduction. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How does green manuring help with iron deficiency in rice?
output: Dhaincha green manuring specifically ameliorates iron deficiency in rice. The decomposing dhaincha biomass releases organic acids and chelates that mobilize soil iron into plant-available forms. This is especially helpful in Punjab alkaline soils where iron deficiency commonly causes yellowing of new rice leaves. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I incorporate rice straw back into the soil?
output: Yes, continuous incorporation or retention of rice straw improves soil health and rice yield over time. After 8 years of continuous straw retention, OR whenever soil organic carbon content reaches the high category per soil test, reduce urea by 20 kg per acre in rice. The savings come from improved nitrogen mineralization in the more biologically active soil. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When can I save 20 kg urea per acre on my rice?
output: Reduce urea by 20 kg per acre in rice when EITHER soil organic carbon content reaches the high category per soil test report, OR after 8 years of continuous rice straw incorporation/retention. Both conditions reflect well-built soil organic matter that mineralizes more nitrogen on its own, reducing external N requirement. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I transplant rice in Punjab?
output: Transplant rice seedlings from 20 June to 10 July for maximum yield and timely field vacation for wheat sowing. Time of transplanting is a single factor that influences rice yield substantially. Earlier transplanting violates the Punjab Subsoil Water Preservation Act and accelerates groundwater depletion; later transplanting risks heat stress and delays the wheat schedule. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I need to transplant late this year. Which rice variety should I prefer?
output: Under late transplanting conditions, prefer PR 126. However, do not transplant PR 126 beyond 15 July - past this date, ripening becomes uneven, grain moisture content rises beyond the permissible level, and yield/quality drop. The 93-day duration of PR 126 makes it the most suitable variety for late transplanting within the 15 July boundary. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What age of seedlings should I use for transplanting medium-duration rice varieties?
output: Use 30-35 days old seedlings for medium-duration rice varieties (PR 131, PR 130, PR 132, PR 133, etc.). For the short-duration variety PR 126, use 25-30 days old seedlings instead. Transplanting of aged seedlings (older than these ranges) results in reduction of yield and grain quality. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What age of seedlings should I use for PR 126 rice?
output: Use 25-30 days old seedlings for PR 126. This is shorter than the 30-35 days used for medium-duration varieties because PR 126 itself is a short-duration variety (93 days after transplanting), and aged seedlings would consume too much of its limited cycle, reducing yield and quality. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I uproot rice seedlings for transplanting?
output: Irrigate the nursery before uprooting to soften the soil and reduce root damage. After uprooting, wash the seedlings in water to remove mud. Clean roots establish faster in the puddled main field, reducing transplanting shock. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I inoculate rice seedlings with biofertilizer?
output: Mix one half kg packet of Azospirillum biofertilizer with 100 litres of water. Dip the roots of rice nursery seedlings for one acre in this solution for 45 minutes, then transplant immediately. Azospirillum is a free-living nitrogen-fixing bacterium that supplements the rice nitrogen requirement. Available at PAU Seed Shop, Gate No. 1, Ludhiana, and Krishi Vigyan Kendras. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What plant spacing should I use for transplanting rice?
output: For normal transplanting of all rice varieties and for late transplanting of PR 126, use 20 x 15 cm spacing (33 hills per sq m). For late transplanting of other varieties, use 15 x 15 cm spacing (44 hills per sq m). Place 2 seedlings per hill. Transplant upright at 2-3 cm depth. This ensures good establishment and early tillering. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How many seedlings should I put in each hill when transplanting rice?
output: Put 2 seedlings per hill when transplanting rice. Transplant upright at 2-3 cm depth. More seedlings per hill leads to overcrowding and weaker tillering; fewer leaves the hill prone to gaps if one seedling fails to establish. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How deep should I transplant rice seedlings?
output: Transplant rice seedlings upright at 2-3 cm depth. Shallower transplanting increases the risk of seedlings floating up; deeper transplanting delays tillering and reduces yield. The 2-3 cm depth balances good anchoring with rapid early growth. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Can I transplant rice on ridges or beds without puddling?
output: Yes, in heavy textured soils. After field preparation and basal fertilizer, prepare ridges or beds with a ridger or wheat bed planter. For 60 cm spaced ridges, transplant seedlings on the middle of the slopes (both sides) at 10 cm plant-to-plant spacing. For 67.5 cm spaced beds, use 9 cm plant-to-plant spacing. Irrigate furrows immediately and transplant. This saves significant irrigation water versus flat puddled transplanting. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How should I irrigate ridge-transplanted rice?
output: For the first 15 days after transplanting on ridges or beds, apply irrigation daily. Thereafter, apply irrigation in furrows only TWO days after the ponded water has infiltrated into the soil. Take care that the field does not develop cracks in the furrows - cracks lose water through deep percolation. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I control weeds in ridge-transplanted rice?
output: Spray 120 mL per acre Nominee Gold or Wash out or Taarak or Macho 10 SC (bispyribac) in 150 litres of water 20-25 days after transplanting. Hand pulling of weeds can also be done if needed. Otherwise follow the same cultural practices as recommended for flat puddled transplanted rice. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What spacing does a mechanical paddy transplanter use?
output: Mechanical paddy transplanters and remotely controlled 2-wheel paddy transplanters transplant rice mat-type nursery at 30 x 12 cm spacing. This wider spacing than manual transplanting (20 x 15 cm) is determined by the machine's mechanical design but still gives adequate plant population. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the most water-saving way to transplant rice in heavy soil?
output: Ridge or bed transplanting without puddling saves significant irrigation water in heavy textured soils. Use 60 cm spaced ridges (10 cm plant spacing on slopes) or 67.5 cm spaced beds (9 cm plant spacing). Daily irrigation for first 15 days, then irrigate furrows 2 days after ponded water infiltrates. Combined with bispyribac herbicide at 20-25 days, this works as well as flat puddled transplanting with much less water. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why is timely transplanting so important for rice yield?
output: Time of transplanting is a single factor that influences rice yield substantially. PAU calls it the most important variable. Delays push the grain-fill stage into October cooler weather, reducing yield, while too-early transplanting accelerates groundwater depletion (illegal in Punjab before 10 June) and worsens stem borer build-up. The 20 June to 10 July window balances all these factors. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Where can I buy Azospirillum biofertilizer for my rice in Punjab?
output: Azospirillum biofertilizer for rice seedling root dip is available at the PAU Seed Shop at Gate No. 1, Ludhiana, and through the Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) and Farm Advisory Service Centres located in different districts of Punjab. One half kg packet inoculates seedlings for one acre of transplanted rice. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What does flat puddled transplanting mean for rice?
output: Flat puddled transplanting is the standard rice transplanting method - the field is puddled (worked with water and tilled to break soil structure) into a flat surface, then seedlings are transplanted in lines at 20 x 15 cm spacing (33 hills per sq m), or 15 x 15 cm (44 hills per sq m) for late transplanting. Place 2 seedlings per hill, upright, at 2-3 cm depth. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How does the 15 x 15 cm spacing for late rice transplanting differ from normal?
output: For late transplanting of varieties other than PR 126, use 15 x 15 cm spacing (44 hills per sq m) instead of the normal 20 x 15 cm (33 hills per sq m). The tighter spacing increases plant density to compensate for the shorter remaining season. PR 126 in late transplanting still uses 20 x 15 cm because its short cycle is designed for late conditions. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I use the paddy weeder in my rice field?
output: Use the paddy weeder for inter-cultural weeding 15 days after transplanting, and again after another fortnight (around 30 days after transplanting). The PAU paddy weeder is a manual implement that disturbs young weeds while aerating the soil. Where a paddy weeder cannot be run (small plots or stubborn terrain), hand weeding can substitute. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why does PAU recommend chemical weed control for rice?
output: PAU notes that controlling weeds with herbicides is both efficient AND economical compared to manual or mechanical weeding alone. The pre-emergence and early post-emergence herbicides effectively control swank (the major rice weed) and provide moderate control of other weeds. Use hand gloves while applying these herbicides. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is swank weed and why is it the main rice weed problem?
output: Swank (Echinochloa) is the major weed of transplanted rice in Punjab. It germinates aggressively under flooded conditions, competes directly with rice for nitrogen and light, and severely reduces yield if not controlled. PAU's pre-emergence and early post-emergence herbicide recommendations are designed primarily to control swank, with moderate effect on other weeds. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How and when should I apply Butachlor in transplanted rice?
output: Apply 1200 mL per acre of Butachlor 50 EC (sold under brands Machete, Delchlor, Punch, Hiltachlor, Teer, Trapp, Milchlor, Banweed, etc.) by mixing with 60 kg of sand per acre. Broadcast in standing water within 2-3 days of transplanting. Butachlor is highly effective against swank and provides moderate control of other weeds. Use hand gloves during application. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Which herbicide is best for kanki control in rice?
output: Anilofos has an edge over other herbicides for kanki control. Apply 850 mL per acre of Arozin 18 EC, OR 500 mL per acre of Arozin 30 EC (also sold as Aniloguard, Libra, Control H-30, Pestoanilofos, Markanil, Jaifos, Haragro-anilfos, Padigard). Mix with 60 kg sand per acre, broadcast in standing water within 2-3 days of transplanting. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I apply Stomp herbicide in transplanted rice?
output: Apply Stomp 30 EC (pendimethalin) at 1000-1200 mL per acre, mixed with 60 kg sand per acre, broadcast in standing water within 2-3 days of transplanting. Use the lower dose (1000 mL) on light textured soils and the higher dose (1200 mL) on medium to heavy textured soils. It controls swank and moderate broadleaf weeds. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is Granite herbicide and when do I apply it in rice?
output: Granite 240 SC (penoxsulam) is an early post-emergence herbicide for transplanted rice. Apply 40 mL per acre at 10-12 days after transplanting in 150 litres of water. It is particularly useful where continuous standing water is a problem, and provides effective control of grass weeds including swank, paddy mothas, AND broadleaf weeds. Do not spray in standing water; apply irrigation one day after spray. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I apply herbicide in standing water in my rice field?
output: It depends on the herbicide. Pre-emergence herbicides like Butachlor, Anilofos, Stomp (pendimethalin), Pretilachlor, and Pyrazosulfuron must be applied in standing water (within 2-3 days of transplanting) by mixing with 60 kg sand per acre. Post-emergence herbicides like Granite (penoxsulam), Nominee Gold (bispyribac), Ricestar, Algrip, etc. should NOT be sprayed in standing water - drain first, spray, and irrigate one day after spray. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I apply post-emergence herbicide in transplanted rice?
output: Apply post-emergence herbicides at 20-25 days after transplanting, when weed plants are at the 2-4 leaf stage. Dissolve the recommended dose in 150 litres of water per acre. Do NOT spray in standing water - drain first. Apply irrigation one day after spray to allow herbicide uptake. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Which herbicide controls Leptochloa (chini gha) in rice?
output: Apply 400 mL per acre of Ricestar 6.7 EC (fenoxaprop-p-ethyl) in 150 litres of water at 20-25 days after transplanting, when weeds are at 2-4 leaf stage. Ricestar is specifically effective against chini gha (Leptochloa) and kanki. Do not spray in standing water; irrigate one day after spray. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I control paddy mothas and broadleaf weeds in rice?
output: Several PAU-recommended options for paddy mothas and broadleaf weeds (ghrilla, sanni etc.): 30 g per acre Algrip 20 WG (metsulfuron), or 50 g per acre Sunrice 15 WG (ethoxysulfuron), or 40 g per acre Londex 60 DF (bensulfuron methyl), or 8 g per acre Almix 20 WP (metsulfuron methyl 10% plus chlorimuron ethyl 10%). Apply at 20-25 days after transplanting in 150 litres of water, weeds at 2-4 leaf stage. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the most broad-spectrum herbicide for transplanted rice?
output: Novixid 3.25 OD (florpyrauxifen-benzyl 1.31% + penoxsulam 2.1%) is the most broad-spectrum option PAU lists. Apply 500 mL per acre at 20-25 days after transplanting in 150 litres of water. It controls swank, multiple paddy mothas (chhatri wala motha, dodiyan wala motha, ghuien), AND broadleaf weeds in a single spray. Do not apply in standing water; irrigate one day after spray. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is Eketsu herbicide and when do I apply it?
output: Eketsu 43 WG is a post-emergence herbicide containing bispyribac sodium 38% plus chlorimuron ethyl 2.5% plus metsulfuron methyl 2.5%. Apply 40 g per acre dissolved in 150 litres of water at 20-25 days after transplanting, when weeds are at 2-4 leaf stage. Effective against swank, paddy mothas including gandi wala motha, and broadleaf weeds. Do not spray in standing water; irrigate one day after spray. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is Sathi herbicide and how do I use it?
output: Sathi 10 WP (pyrazosulfuron ethyl) is a pre-emergence herbicide. Apply 60 g per acre by mixing with 60 kg of sand per acre, broadcast in standing water within 2-3 days of transplanting. It controls swank and provides moderate control of other weeds. Use hand gloves while applying. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is Rifit and when do I apply it?
output: Rifit 50 EC (pretilachlor) is a pre-emergence herbicide also sold as Eraze, Markpretila, Revenge, Mif Pretila, or Sokusai. Apply 600 mL per acre, OR use Rifit Plus 37 EW at 750 mL per acre. Mix with 60 kg of sand per acre, broadcast in standing water within 2-3 days of transplanting. Effective against swank with moderate control of other weeds. Use hand gloves. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I wear protective equipment when applying rice herbicides?
output: Yes - PAU specifically instructs to use hand gloves while applying these herbicides (Butachlor, Anilofos, Stomp, Pretilachlor, Sathi, etc.). Even though these are routine agricultural herbicides, skin contact can cause irritation and chronic exposure has health risks. Wear long sleeves and avoid spraying into the wind. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When is the optimum weed plant stage to apply post-emergence herbicide in rice?
output: Apply post-emergence herbicides when weed plants are at the 2-4 leaf stage, typically 20-25 days after transplanting. Younger weeds may not have absorbed enough herbicide to die; older weeds (5+ leaves) are harder to kill and require higher doses. The 2-4 leaf window gives best efficacy at recommended doses. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I plan rice weed control across the season?
output: Three-step PAU plan: (1) Pre-emergence within 2-3 days of transplanting: Butachlor (1200 mL/acre) or Anilofos (850 mL of 18 EC, or 500 mL of 30 EC) or Stomp (1000-1200 mL) or Pretilachlor (600 mL of 50 EC, 750 mL of Rifit Plus) mixed with 60 kg sand, broadcast in standing water. (2) Optional early post-emergence at 10-12 days: 40 mL Granite in 150 L water, especially for problem standing water. (3) Post-emergence at 20-25 days when weeds at 2-4 leaf stage: Nominee Gold, Ricestar, Algrip, Almix, Novixid, or Eketsu in 150 L water, no standing water. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why does PAU say to rotate herbicide groups in rice?
output: PAU specifically recommends using different groups of recommended herbicides in rotation to avoid herbicide resistance in weeds. Continuous use of the same herbicide group selects for resistant weed populations, eventually making it useless. Rotate among Butachlor, Anilofos, Pretilachlor, Bispyribac, Penoxsulam, and other groups across seasons. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What happens if I delay applying herbicide on my rice?
output: Delay in application of herbicides results in poor control of weeds. Pre-emergence herbicides must be applied within 2-3 days of transplanting; early post-emergence within 10-12 days; post-emergence by 20-25 days when weeds are at 2-4 leaf stage.
