Beyond these windows, weed plants are too established for the recommended doses to kill them efficiently, leading to yield loss and stronger weed populations next season. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much urea should I save if I apply farmyard manure to my rice?
output: Apply 6 tonnes of farmyard manure per acre and save 16 kg of nitrogen (35 kg urea) from the recommended fertilizer dose. The FYM also improves soil structure, organic carbon, and micronutrient availability. PAU recommends applying organic manures alongside chemical fertilizers for higher yield and soil health. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much urea can I save with press mud or poultry manure on my rice?
output: Both press mud (6 tonnes per acre) and poultry manure (2.5 tonnes per acre) save 25 kg of nitrogen (55 kg urea) per acre - more savings than FYM. Press mud and poultry manure are more nutrient-dense than farmyard manure. Apply before transplanting along with the reduced urea dose. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much urea do I save with prali char on my rice?
output: Apply 2.0 tonnes of prali char (paddy straw biochar) per acre and save 16 kg of nitrogen (35 kg urea) per acre. Bonus: prali char also increases crop yield by 10 percent on top of the urea savings. This is the highest yield-boosting option among PAU's organic amendments and turns paddy straw waste into a productive input rather than burning. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much fertilizer does green manure save in rice?
output: Green manuring (dhaincha, cowpea, or sunnhemp incorporated 6-8 weeks old, one day before transplanting) saves 25 kg of nitrogen (55 kg urea) per acre. Summer moong residue incorporation saves 16 kg N (35 kg urea). The green manure also improves soil structure and supplies micronutrients. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I have coarse textured (sandy) soil. How do I manage rice fertility?
output: On coarse textured soils, apply organic manures (6 tonnes FYM, OR 2.5 tonnes poultry manure, OR 6 tonnes pressmud, OR 2.5 tonnes rice straw compost per acre) or green manure or summer moong residue IN ADDITION TO the recommended dose of nitrogen. The standard 'reduce urea by X kg' table doesn't apply on sandy soils because they leak nitrogen and need full fertilizer plus the organic boost. This also ameliorates micronutrient deficiencies common in sandy rice-wheat fields. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much chemical fertilizer should I apply to my rice?
output: Without a soil test, PAU recommends 42 kg N, 12 kg P2O5, and 12 kg K2O per acre for all rice varieties EXCEPT PR 132. For PR 132 (nitrogen-efficient variety), use only 31.5 kg N. Sources: 90 kg neem-coated urea per acre (67.5 kg for PR 132), 27 kg DAP or 75 kg single superphosphate, and 20 kg muriate of potash. Apply phosphorus and potash only if soil tests low. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How is the fertilizer dose for PR 132 rice different from other varieties?
output: PR 132 needs only 31.5 kg N per acre, 25 percent less than other varieties (42 kg). That translates to 67.5 kg neem-coated urea instead of 90 kg. Phosphorus (12 kg P2O5) and potassium (12 kg K2O) requirements stay the same. Higher nitrogen on PR 132 risks lodging without yield benefit. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When and how should I apply phosphorus to rice?
output: Apply the whole of phosphorus and potassium before puddling, based on soil test. If you missed pre-puddling, phosphorus can be top-dressed up to 21 days after transplanting. PAU also says skip phosphorus application to rice IF the recommended dose was applied to the preceding wheat crop - residual phosphorus carries over. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What if I use 27 kg DAP for rice phosphorus?
output: When 27 kg DAP per acre is used as the phosphorus source in deficient soil, reduce the urea dose by 10 kg per acre. DAP contains 18 percent nitrogen alongside phosphorus, so applying full urea on top would over-supply nitrogen and risk lodging. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How should I split nitrogen application across the rice growing season?
output: Apply nitrogen in three equal splits to all recommended rice varieties. First split: within 7 days of transplanting. Second split: at 21 days after transplanting. Third split: timed to the variety's growth (short-duration varieties get the third split earlier than long-duration varieties). Splits prevent nitrogen leaching loss in flooded paddy and match supply to crop demand. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I apply the first nitrogen split to my transplanted rice?
output: Apply the first nitrogen split within 7 days of transplanting. This jump-starts tillering during early establishment when nitrogen demand is high but the seedlings can take up only what is in their immediate root zone. Use one-third of the total recommended nitrogen for the variety. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I apply the second nitrogen split to rice?
output: Apply the second nitrogen split at 21 days after transplanting. This boosts active tillering, which directly determines yield through panicle number per square metre. Use one-third of the total recommended nitrogen for the variety. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Can I save fertilizer by applying organic manure to my rice?
output: Yes. PAU specifies these urea savings per acre with organic amendments: 6 tonnes FYM saves 35 kg urea (16 kg N), 6 tonnes pressmud saves 55 kg urea (25 kg N), 2.5 tonnes poultry manure saves 55 kg urea, 2.4 tonnes gobar gas slurry saves 35 kg urea, 2.0 tonnes prali char saves 35 kg urea AND boosts yield 10 percent, green manure saves 55 kg urea, summer moong residue saves 35 kg urea. Note: do NOT apply these savings on coarse-textured (sandy) soils where you should add organic plus full N. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I reduce sterility in my rice?
output: Apply foliar spray of 1.5 percent potassium nitrate (3 kg potassium nitrate dissolved in 200 litres of water per acre) at the boot stage of the rice crop. Sterility - empty grains - results from heat stress or nutrient imbalance during panicle initiation; the potassium nitrate spray strengthens the developing florets and improves grain set. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What boot stage spray helps rice grain filling?
output: Apply 1.5 percent potassium nitrate foliar spray (3 kg potassium nitrate in 200 litres of water per acre) at the boot stage to reduce sterility and improve grain set. The boot stage is when the panicle is fully formed inside the flag leaf sheath, just before emergence - the most heat-sensitive and nutrient-demanding period. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What organic options work alongside chemical fertilizer in rice for soil health?
output: PAU recommends combining chemical fertilizers with: farmyard manure, pressmud, poultry manure, gobar gas plant slurry, prali char (paddy straw biochar), green manure (dhaincha/cowpea/sunnhemp), or summer moong residue incorporation. Each option has documented urea savings (16-25 kg N saved per acre) and improves soil organic carbon over time. Bio-fertilizer like Azospirillum (root dip before transplanting) adds free nitrogen fixation. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I apply the third nitrogen split for PR 126 rice?
output: Apply the third nitrogen split for PR 126 (the short-duration variety) at 35 days after transplanting. This is earlier than other varieties because PR 126 matures in just 93 days, so the late-stage nitrogen demand peaks sooner. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I apply the third nitrogen split for medium-duration rice varieties?
output: For all varieties other than PR 126, apply the third nitrogen split at 42 days after transplanting. PR 126 (short-duration, 93 days) gets its third split earlier at 35 days. The 42-day timing matches the panicle initiation and stem elongation period when nitrogen demand peaks for medium-duration varieties. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I apply urea in standing water?
output: No - apply the second and third nitrogen splits when water is NOT standing in the field. Drain or let the field dry first, broadcast the urea, then irrigate on the third day of fertilizer application. Applying in standing water leads to ammonia volatilization losses and reduces nitrogen use efficiency. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I want to use fish pond sediments in my rice field. How do I adjust fertilizer?
output: If you apply 6 tonnes per acre of fish pond sediments before transplanting paddy, reduce the recommended fertilizer dose by 25 percent. Fish pond sediments are rich in nutrients accumulated from the pond ecosystem and supplement chemical fertilizer. The 25 percent reduction applies across nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I use PAU-LCC for need-based urea on my rice?
output: Apply basal dose of 25 kg urea per acre at puddling. Start matching colour of the first fully exposed leaf from the top with the LCC at 7-day intervals starting 14 days after transplanting. If 6 or more out of 10 leaves are LIGHTER than LCC shade 4, apply 25 kg urea per acre. If colour equals or is darker than LCC shade 4, apply NO urea. Discontinue LCC use after flowering initiation. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What basal urea dose should I apply at puddling for rice?
output: Apply 25 kg urea per acre as basal dose at puddling when using PAU-LCC for need-based nitrogen management. Subsequent urea applications are decided by leaf colour readings every 7 days after the 14th day of transplanting - apply 25 kg/acre only when 6+ of 10 leaves are lighter than LCC shade 4. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Does PAU-LCC work for all rice varieties?
output: Yes - need-based nitrogen management using LCC holds good for ALL prevalent rice varieties grown in ALL types of soils in Punjab. It is especially beneficial for optimum nitrogen use when fields are amended with organic manures (FYM, pressmud, prali char, green manure, etc.) where prediction of soil N supply is harder. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I correctly read PAU-LCC for rice?
output: Three rules from PAU: (1) Always match leaf colour under the shade of your body, not in direct sun. (2) Selected leaves should be free of insect-pest incidence. (3) The crop should not be under water stress and other nutrients (P, K, Zn) should be supplied per recommendations. Match the first fully exposed leaf from the top of 10 representative plants. If 6 or more are lighter than shade 4, apply 25 kg urea per acre. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I stop using LCC and stop applying urea on rice?
output: Discontinue LCC use AND stop applying urea after the initiation of flowering. By flowering, the rice has set its yield potential through tillering and panicle initiation; further urea would cause lodging without yield benefit and may delay maturity. The grain-filling stage uses internal nitrogen translocation. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Where can I buy PAU-LCC for rice?
output: PAU-LCC is available at the PAU Seed Shop at Gate No. 1, Ludhiana, AND through Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) and Farm Advisory Service Centres in different districts of Punjab. The same chart is used for both rice and wheat with different shade thresholds. It is inexpensive and pays back many times in saved urea costs. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What does zinc deficiency look like in rice?
output: Zinc deficiency symptoms appear 2-3 weeks after transplanting. Lower leaves become rusty brown near the base and ultimately dry up. Seedlings with zinc deficiency remain stunted and tillerless. The symptoms are common in alkaline Punjab soils. Apply zinc sulphate immediately when symptoms appear or preventively at puddling if previous crops on the same field had shown deficiency. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I correct zinc deficiency in my rice?
output: Apply 25 kg of zinc sulphate heptahydrate (21 percent Zn) per acre, OR 16 kg of zinc sulphate monohydrate (33 percent Zn) per acre at puddling if previous crop showed deficiency. If symptoms appear in growing crop, apply this same quantity as soon as possible. For deteriorated soils where deficiency persists in patches, broadcast 10 kg zinc sulphate heptahydrate or 6.5 kg zinc sulphate monohydrate per acre mixed with equal dry soil on affected patches only. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I see lower leaves of my rice turning rusty brown near the base. What's wrong?
output: This is classic zinc deficiency in rice, common 2-3 weeks after transplanting on Punjab alkaline soils. Apply 25 kg zinc sulphate heptahydrate (21 percent Zn) or 16 kg zinc sulphate monohydrate (33 percent Zn) per acre as soon as possible. The seedlings will be stunted and tillerless if untreated, hurting yield severely. For preventive treatment in repeat-deficient fields, apply at puddling next season. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What if zinc deficiency keeps appearing in patches even after I applied zinc sulphate?
output: On highly deteriorated soils, zinc deficiency sometimes returns in patches despite the recommended pre-puddling application. Spot-treat affected patches: broadcast 10 kg zinc sulphate heptahydrate per acre OR 6.5 kg zinc sulphate monohydrate per acre, mixed with equal quantity of dry soil, only on the affected areas. This targets correction without over-applying to the whole field. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Is 21 percent or 33 percent zinc sulphate better for rice?
output: Both work at PAU-equivalent rates. For pre-puddling or growing-crop deficiency: 25 kg zinc sulphate heptahydrate (21 percent Zn) OR 16 kg zinc sulphate monohydrate (33 percent Zn) per acre. For patch correction: 10 kg heptahydrate OR 6.5 kg monohydrate. The 33 percent monohydrate is more concentrated, saves transport and storage, and has gained popularity. Both supply similar elemental zinc when applied at the equivalent rates. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What does iron deficiency look like in rice?
output: Iron deficiency in rice shows as chlorosis (yellowing) of the youngest leaf about three weeks after transplanting. It typically appears under water-scarce conditions when iron uptake is hampered. Plants die and often the crop fails completely if untreated. Start giving copious irrigations as soon as chlorosis appears - water restoration usually resolves the deficiency. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: My rice's youngest leaves are turning yellow at three weeks. What's wrong?
output: This pattern - chlorosis in the youngest leaf at about 3 weeks after transplanting - indicates iron deficiency, typically triggered by water scarcity. Start copious irrigations immediately as soon as chlorosis appears. If untreated, plants die and the crop can fail completely. Dhaincha green manure preceding rice also reduces iron deficiency risk. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I prevent iron deficiency in rice?
output: Iron deficiency in rice is triggered by water scarcity. Maintain adequate irrigation - especially during the first 3 weeks after transplanting. Dhaincha green manuring before rice also ameliorates iron deficiency by mobilizing soil iron. If chlorosis appears in youngest leaves at week 3, give copious irrigations immediately. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I treat iron deficiency in rice with foliar spray?
output: Apply 2 or 3 sprays of 1 percent ferrous sulphate solution at weekly intervals - that is 1 kg of ferrous sulphate dissolved in 100 litres of water per acre. Start as soon as you see chlorosis in the youngest leaves. Combine with copious irrigation to address the underlying water scarcity that triggered the deficiency. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How long should I keep water standing in my rice field after transplanting?
output: Keep water standing continuously for only TWO WEEKS after transplanting so seedlings get properly established. After that, apply irrigation two days after the ponded water has infiltrated into the soil. The depth of standing water should not exceed 10 cm. Continuous flooding wastes water without yield benefit. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How can I use a tensiometer to save irrigation water in rice?
output: Install a tensiometer at 15-20 cm soil depth. Irrigate when soil matric tension reaches 150 plus or minus 20 cm, OR when the water level in the tensiometer enters the yellow strip. This is precision irrigation timing - water is applied only when the soil actually needs it, saving significant water without yield reduction. Take care that the field does not develop cracks. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the maximum depth of standing water I should keep in my rice field?
output: The depth of standing water should not exceed 10 cm in transplanted rice. Deeper water wastes irrigation, reduces oxygen in the root zone, and can promote rotting of the lower stems. After the establishment period (first 2 weeks of continuous flooding), maintain shallow standing water with intermittent irrigation. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I drain my rice field before weeding?
output: Yes - drain away excess water before interculturing or weeding operations, then irrigate the field again after the operation. Working in standing water makes weeding harder and damages young rice tillers. Drain shortly before, do the work, then re-flood. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I stop irrigating rice before harvest?
output: Stop irrigation about a fortnight (15 days) before maturity. This allows the field to dry enough for combine harvesting and lets the wheat or other rabi crop be sown on schedule. Continued late irrigation delays harvest, makes combine operation impossible without rutting, and risks pushing wheat sowing past the optimum window. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What happens if I delay harvesting my rice past dead ripe stage?
output: Delayed harvest past dead ripe causes shattering of grains - mature grains fall to the ground and are lost. Milling quality of the grains is also affected: more breakage and lower head rice recovery. Harvest as soon as ears are nearly ripened and straw has turned yellow, even if other field operations compete for time. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Can I use a combine harvester for paddy?
output: Yes - combines are successfully used for harvesting paddy. Operate the combine at the proper speed for clean threshing without grain damage. Prefer combines fitted with a PAU Super SMS (Straw Management System) for chopping and even distribution of straw across the field. After SMS-equipped combine harvest, wheat can be directly sown with Happy Seeder without burning paddy straw. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the PAU Super SMS and why should I use it on my combine?
output: The PAU Super SMS (Straw Management System) is a combine attachment that chops paddy straw into small pieces and distributes them evenly across the field during harvest. After SMS-equipped combine harvest, the field is ready for direct wheat sowing with Happy Seeder - no straw burning required. This solves the air pollution crisis caused by paddy straw burning while saving labour and time before wheat sowing. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I sow wheat after rice without burning paddy straw?
output: Use a combine fitted with a PAU Super SMS (Straw Management System) to harvest paddy. The SMS chops straw and distributes it evenly across the field during harvest. Then directly sow wheat with a Happy Seeder, which cuts through the residue and seeds wheat in one pass. No burning needed. This is PAU's recommended approach for solving the paddy straw burning problem. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What other equipment can I use for harvesting paddy besides combine?
output: Tractor-drawn vertical conveyor reaper windrower can also be used for harvesting paddy. Multi-crop threshers can be used for threshing the harvested paddy. See Annexure V of the PAU Package of Practices for the full equipment list. Combines with PAU Super SMS remain the most efficient option for large fields. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I produce pure seed of my rice variety on my own farm?
output: Select a good plot of standing rice crop and rogue it thoroughly - remove all admixture plants and diseased plants. Harvest and thresh this plot separately from the main field. Dry the produce well and store separately in disinfested bins. This farm-saved pure seed maintains varietal identity and disease-free status for your next sowing. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is roguing and why do I do it for rice seed production?
output: Roguing is the process of inspecting your standing rice crop and physically removing any off-type plants (different variety mix-ins) and diseased plants before harvest. Walk through the plot multiple times during the season. Removing these undesirable plants ensures the seed you save next year is pure to the variety and free from seed-borne diseases. Combined with separate harvest, threshing, and storage, roguing maintains seed quality. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the maximum allowed moisture content for rice marketing?
output: As per specified norms, paddy moisture content should not exceed 17 percent at the time of marketing. Higher moisture risks rejection or price docking. Drier produce stores better and brings full price. Use sun drying or thresher fan to bring moisture down before taking to market. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What charges should I pay when marketing my rice?
output: As per the specified norms in Punjab, the farmer pays only unloading and cleaning charges on the produce delivered to the market. Other commission and handling charges are paid by the buyer. Get a J form from the commission agent as proof of sale. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the J form for rice marketing?
output: The J form is the official sale receipt issued by the commission agent (arhtia) when you sell paddy in a Punjab mandi. PAU advises farmers to always obtain the J form from the commission agent because it serves as proof of sale, supports MSP claims, and is needed for various government schemes and subsidy applications. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why does PAU say excessive nitrogen at flowering causes yield loss?
output: Excessive nitrogen during flowering causes sterility - empty grains in the panicle - and consequently heavy reduction in yield. The lush canopy from over-fertilization also lodges and shades developing panicles. PAU's split application schedule (third split at 35-42 days, NO urea after flowering, LCC stops at flowering) is designed to prevent this damage. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the best moisture content for storing my paddy?
output: The optimum moisture content for paddy storage is 12 percent. Dry the produce in the sun for about a week before storing in bins or in a heap inside a room. At 12 percent moisture, paddy resists fungal growth, insect attack, and grain quality deterioration during storage. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I store paddy at home for my own use?
output: Dry the paddy thoroughly in the sun for about a week, bringing moisture down to 12 percent. Store either in metal/plastic bins or in a heap inside a closed room. Disinfest the storage area before filling. Higher moisture risks weevils, fungus, and rot during the storage period. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much paddy straw is produced in Punjab each year?
output: Punjab produces about 220 lakh tonnes of paddy straw annually. A large portion is currently burnt by farmers, causing massive air pollution and nutrient loss. The straw contains significant amounts of plant nutrients - burning one tonne loses 400 kg organic carbon, 5.5 kg N, 2.3 kg P, 25 kg K, and 1.2 kg S. PAU strongly recommends in-situ or ex-situ management instead of burning. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What nutrients do I lose when I burn one tonne of paddy straw?
output: Burning one tonne of paddy straw causes loss of 400 kg organic carbon, 5.5 kg of nitrogen, 2.3 kg of phosphorus, 25 kg of potassium, and 1.2 kg of sulphur. Burning causes complete loss of nitrogen and sulphur. Beyond nutrient cost, burning releases carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, methane, and nitric oxide - all harmful to human and animal health. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why is burning paddy straw bad for health?
output: Burning paddy straw produces carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, methane, and nitric oxide - all harmful to human and animal health. The smoke contributes to north India's severe winter air pollution and causes respiratory illnesses across hundreds of kilometres. PAU recommends in-situ residue management (Happy Seeder, Super Seeder, Smart Seeder, surface seeding) or ex-situ uses to eliminate burning. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is Happy Seeder and how does it help avoid paddy straw burning?
output: Happy Seeder is a PAU-recommended machine that sows wheat in combine-harvested paddy fields WITHOUT any straw burning. It is a PTO-driven machine operated by a 45 HP tractor, covering 0.75 to 0.80 acre per hour. The loose straw needs to be spread uniformly first - either manually or by harvesting paddy with a combine fitted with PAU Super SMS. The paddy straw then acts as mulch, suppressing weeds. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How fast does Happy Seeder cover wheat sowing?
output: Happy Seeder covers about 0.75 to 0.80 acre per hour when operated with a 45 HP tractor. So a 5-acre wheat field takes about 6-7 hours of operation. The PTO-driven machine cuts through paddy stubble and sows wheat in one pass without burning the straw. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is Super Seeder and how is it different from Happy Seeder?
output: Super Seeder is a PTO-driven wheat sowing machine for combine-harvested paddy fields, operated by a 55 HP or higher tractor. It covers 4.5 to 5.5 acre per day - faster than Happy Seeder (0.75-0.80 acre per hour, about 6 acre in a day). Super Seeder requires harvesting the paddy with a combine fitted with PAU Super SMS first. No straw burning is needed with either machine. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the PAU Smart Seeder?
output: PAU Smart Seeder is a wheat sowing machine for combine-harvested paddy fields, PTO-driven and operated by a 45 HP or higher tractor. It covers 7 to 8 acre per day - the fastest among PAU's residue-management seeders. Requires combine harvest with PAU Super SMS. Like Happy Seeder and Super Seeder, it eliminates the need for straw burning. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What tractor HP do I need for Happy Seeder, Super Seeder, and Smart Seeder?
output: Happy Seeder: 45 HP tractor (covers 0.75-0.80 acre per hour). Super Seeder: 55 HP or higher (4.5-5.5 acre per day). PAU Smart Seeder: 45 HP or higher (7-8 acre per day). All three are PTO-driven and require paddy to be harvested with a combine fitted with PAU Super SMS, OR manual spreading of straw, before operation. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Which is the fastest PAU paddy-residue wheat seeder?
output: PAU Smart Seeder is the fastest at 7-8 acre per day, beating Super Seeder (4.5-5.5 acre per day) and Happy Seeder (about 6 acre per day). All three eliminate paddy straw burning. Smart Seeder runs on 45 HP tractor (same as Happy Seeder) but is more efficient. Choose based on machinery availability and field size. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What if my combine does not have a Super SMS attachment? How do I sow wheat without burning?
output: If paddy is harvested with a combine WITHOUT SMS, use the PAU Straw Cutter cum Spreader for chopping and spreading the paddy straw evenly. After chopping, sow wheat with PAU Happy Seeder fitted with press wheels. This achieves the same no-burn outcome as combine-with-SMS, just with one extra pass for the cutter-spreader. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the PAU Straw Cutter cum Spreader used for?
output: PAU Straw Cutter cum Spreader chops and evenly spreads paddy straw across the field after combine harvest (when the combine does not have an SMS attachment). After this pass, wheat can be sown with PAU Happy Seeder fitted with press wheels - no straw burning required. The machine essentially performs the SMS function as a separate operation. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is surface seeding for wheat after rice?
output: Surface seeding cum mulching is a low-cost easy technique for in-situ paddy residue management with timely-sown wheat. Steps: (1) Broadcast wheat seed and basal fertilizer uniformly in the combine-harvested paddy field. (2) One pass of cutter cum spreader to cut paddy straw at 4-5 inch above soil surface. (3) Irrigation to initiate germination. The straw provides complete mulching, weed infestation is reduced, and no costly machinery is needed beyond the cutter cum spreader. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I do not have access to Happy Seeder. What is a low-cost way to manage paddy straw and sow wheat?
output: Use surface seeding - the lowest-cost in-situ paddy residue management. Broadcast wheat seed and basal fertilizer uniformly in combine-harvested paddy field. Then make one pass with a cutter cum spreader to cut paddy straw at 4-5 inches above the soil. Irrigate to initiate germination. The straw provides full mulching, weed infestation is less, and timely-sown wheat establishes well. No expensive seeder needed. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How does paddy straw mulch help my wheat crop?
output: Paddy straw mulch (left after Happy Seeder, Super Seeder, Smart Seeder, or surface seeding) suppresses weed populations significantly, conserves soil moisture by reducing evaporation, regulates soil temperature, and decomposes over the season to build soil organic matter. PAU specifically notes that the straw mulch adversely affects weed populations - meaning fewer herbicide passes needed. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How is surface seeding wheat different from drilling with Happy Seeder?
output: Surface seeding broadcasts wheat seed AND basal fertilizer on the surface of the combine-harvested paddy field, then a cutter-spreader chops and drops paddy straw at 4-5 inch above soil. Irrigation triggers germination. Happy Seeder physically drills wheat seed below the residue using a PTO-driven 45 HP tractor pass. Surface seeding is cheaper (no expensive seeder), Happy Seeder gives more uniform plant stands. Both eliminate burning. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why does PAU recommend in-situ paddy straw management over burning?
output: Three reasons: (1) Nutrient retention - one tonne of burnt straw loses 400 kg carbon, 5.5 kg N, 2.3 kg P, 25 kg K, 1.2 kg S; in-situ retention puts these back in soil. (2) Air quality - burning produces CO, CO2, methane, nitric oxide, all harmful to human and animal health and contributing to severe regional air pollution. (3) Soil health - long-term retention builds organic carbon, allowing 20 kg urea per acre savings after 8 years or once SOC is high. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is a straw baler and what does it do?
output: A straw baler collects loose paddy straw or complete straw (after chopping standing stubbles with a stubble shaver) and packs it into bales for transport. The bales can be used for power generation, biogas, geyser fuel, phospho-compost, prali char, animal bedding, packaging, or sold to industrial buyers. Baling is the entry step for ex-situ paddy straw management - using straw away from the field. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Can paddy straw be used to generate electricity?
output: Yes - eleven biomass power plants have been established in Punjab specifically for generating electricity from paddy straw bales. The heat from burning paddy straw runs a steam turbine that drives an electricity generator. This converts what was once burnt waste into a productive energy source while solving the air pollution problem. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How many biomass power plants in Punjab use paddy straw?
output: Eleven biomass power plants have been established in Punjab for generating electricity from paddy straw bales. They use the heat from burning paddy straw to run steam turbines that produce electricity. This is one of PAU's recommended ex-situ uses for baled paddy straw, alongside biogas, geyser fuel, phospho-compost, and prali char. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Can I make biogas from paddy straw?
output: Yes - PAU recommends a specially designed biogas plant that uses paddy straw. Fill it one time with 16 quintal chopped paddy straw plus 4-5 quintal cattle dung. The plant then provides 3-4 cubic metres of biogas daily for 3 months. This is enough cooking gas for a small household. After 3 months, refill with the next batch. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much paddy straw and cow dung do I need for a biogas plant?
output: Fill a paddy straw biogas plant one time with 16 quintal of chopped paddy straw along with 4-5 quintal of cattle dung. This single fill produces 3-4 cubic metres of biogas daily for 3 months. After the 3-month cycle, empty and refill with the next batch. The combined feedstock balances the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio for efficient methane production. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is a paddy straw geyser?
output: PAU has developed a geyser that heats water using paddy straw bales as fuel. About 100 litres of water can be heated to 45-50 degrees Celsius in 3-4 hours. The water once filled in the geyser remains hot for up to 24 hours or more thanks to the geyser's insulation. This is a low-cost rural heating solution that uses paddy straw productively instead of burning it in the open. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How much water can a PAU paddy straw geyser heat?
output: A PAU paddy straw geyser heats about 100 litres of water to 45-50 degrees Celsius in 3-4 hours. The heated water stays warm for up to 24 hours or more thanks to insulation. This is enough hot water for daily household use - bathing, washing, cooking - while productively using paddy straw bales that would otherwise be burnt. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Can paddy straw be composted into phospho-compost?
output: Yes - phospho-compost can be prepared from paddy straw. PAU provides full preparation details in the Organic Farming chapter of the Package of Practices. The compost adds both organic matter and bound phosphorus to the soil when later applied to crops. This is one of PAU's recommended ex-situ paddy straw uses alongside power, biogas, geyser, and prali char. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is prali char and how is it prepared?
output: Prali char is a carbon-rich porous product obtained from partial combustion of rice straw at low temperatures with little or no oxygen (a form of biochar). Prepare it in a pyramid or dome-type kiln of bricks and clay. To produce 8 quintals of prali char from 12 quintals of rice straw, build a 14 ft tall dome with 10 ft diameter. Provide two windows each at top and bottom for loading paddy straw, and six vents of 2 inch diameter in the upper portion to control combustion. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What ratio of rice straw to prali char output do I get?
output: From 12 quintals of rice straw, the PAU dome kiln produces 8 quintals of prali char - a 67 percent yield by weight. The carbon-rich biochar can be applied at 2.0 tonnes per acre to wheat (saves 35 kg urea, increases yield 10 percent) or to rice (saves 35 kg urea per acre). Prali char is the highest-value ex-situ paddy straw product for soil health. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What dimensions does the PAU prali char dome kiln need?
output: Build the PAU dome kiln with bricks and clay at 14 ft height and 10 ft diameter to produce 8 quintals of prali char from 12 quintals of rice straw. Provide two loading windows each at the top and bottom of the kiln. Six vents of 2-inch diameter in the upper portion control combustion airflow. The low-oxygen partial combustion preserves carbon as porous biochar rather than burning it to ash. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Summarize the PAU options for managing paddy straw without burning.
output: Two main approaches. IN-SITU (in-field): (a) Wheat sowing with Happy Seeder (45 HP, 0.75-0.80 acre/hour), (b) Super Seeder (55 HP+, 4.5-5.5 acre/day), (c) PAU Smart Seeder (45 HP+, 7-8 acre/day), (d) Surface seeding with PAU Surface Seeder, (e) Incorporation with Straw Chopper cum Spreader plus rotary tillers (2-3 weeks to wattar). EX-SITU (after baling): (a) 11 biomass power plants in Punjab, (b) Biogas plant (16q straw + 4-5q dung gives 3-4 m3 daily for 3 months), (c) PAU paddy straw geyser (100 L hot water in 3-4 hours), (d) Phospho-compost, (e) Prali char (8q output from 12q straw, dome kiln). Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I operate a prali char dome kiln?
output: Fill the kiln with rice straw up to the top. Seal the lower loading window. Ignite the straw from the top loading window and immediately seal it with clay. Partial combustion proceeds from top to bottom. Thin blue smoke from a vent indicates that zone has finished. Seal upper vents first, then middle, then lower as combustion progresses downward. The whole process takes 10-12 hours. Pour diluted clay-and-water mixture on the outer surface to seal cracks and cool the kiln. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I know when prali char is fully formed in a zone of the kiln?
output: Emission of thin blue smoke from the vents indicates the process of prali char formation is complete in that zone. Seal those vents and let combustion proceed downward to the next zone. Repeat for the middle and lower zones. The blue-smoke signal is critical because oversealing causes incomplete combustion and underseal lets the straw burn fully to ash, defeating the purpose. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How long does prali char preparation take?
output: The prali char combustion process takes about 10-12 hours from ignition to completion. After that, the kiln normally takes about 2 days to cool naturally. To speed up cooling and remove prali char on the same day, sprinkle water on the outer surface of the kiln. Plan a 24 to 48 hour total cycle from loading to harvest. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What nutrients does prali char contain?
output: Prali char contains 30-36 percent carbon, 0.5-0.6 percent nitrogen, 0.16-0.22 percent phosphorus, and 1.6-2.2 percent potassium on average. Beyond nutrients, the porous biochar improves soil structure, water retention, and microbial habitat. Application at 2.0 tonnes per acre to rice or wheat saves 16 kg nitrogen (35 kg urea) per acre and increases crop productivity. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Apart from biogas and electricity, what else can I do with paddy straw?
output: Beyond power generation, biogas, geyser fuel, phospho-compost, and prali char, paddy straw can be used as mulch material in different crops, for mushroom cultivation, and as animal bedding. Each of these productive uses keeps straw out of burning, retains its nutrients in agriculture, and reduces north India's air pollution problem. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Can paddy straw be used for mushroom cultivation?
output: Yes - paddy straw is a recognized substrate for mushroom cultivation. PAU lists mushroom cultivation among the productive uses of paddy straw alongside mulch material, animal bedding, biogas, geyser fuel, prali char, phospho-compost, and biomass power. Mushroom growing turns straw into food while preserving nutrients in the spent substrate, which can later be used as compost. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is rice stem borer and what damage does it cause?
output: Rice stem borer larvae bore into the stem and cause damage from July to October. Affected young plants show dead-hearts - yellowing and drying of the central shoot. Older infested plants produce empty earheads (whiteheads) which turn white and stand erect. Both forms cause significant yield loss. The Economic Threshold Level (ETL) is 5 percent dead hearts - spray when this level is reached. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What does rice stem borer damage look like?
output: Two key symptoms. On young plants: dead-hearts - yellowing and drying of the central shoot. On older plants: whiteheads - empty earheads that turn white and stand erect (because the panicle emerged from a damaged stem). Damage occurs from July to October. Spray when dead hearts exceed 5 percent of plants (the Economic Threshold Level). Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the Economic Threshold Level for rice stem borer?
output: The Economic Threshold Level (ETL) for rice stem borer is 5 percent dead hearts. Below this level, spraying is not economically justified - natural enemies and the crop's compensatory tillering handle the damage. At or above 5 percent, apply insecticide. ETL-based spraying minimizes pesticide use, cost, and environmental impact while protecting yield. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What insecticides can I use for rice stem borer?
output: PAU lists 7 options for stem borer control at ETL (5 percent dead hearts) in 100 litres of water per acre: 60 mL Coragen 18.5 SC (chlorantraniliprole), or 20 mL Fame 480 SC (flubendiamide 39.35%), or 50 g Takumi 20 WG (flubendiamide 20%), or 400 g Supremo 50 SP (thiocyclam hydrogen oxalate), or 170 g Mortar 75 SG (cartap hydrochloride), or 1 litre Coroban/Dursban/Lethal/Force 20 EC (chlorpyriphos), or 80 mL Ecotin (azadirachtin 5% neem-based). Prefer Ecotin at pest initiation stage. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the recommended biopesticide for early-stage rice stem borer?
output: Use Ecotin (azadirachtin 5%) - a neem-based biopesticide - at 80 mL in 100 litres of water per acre. PAU specifically prefers Ecotin at the pest initiation stage. It is effective against stem borer when populations are starting to build, has lower environmental impact than synthetic insecticides, and preserves natural predators. For heavy infestations, switch to a synthetic option. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is leaf folder and what damage does it do to rice?
output: Leaf folder larvae fold rice leaves longitudinally and eat the green tissue, leaving white streaks. The damage is highest during August-October. The Economic Threshold Level (ETL) is 10 percent leaf damage - spray when this level is reached. The folded leaves reduce photosynthetic area and harbour the larvae for further damage. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I mechanically control leaf folder in rice without chemicals?
output: Mechanical control of leaf folder is possible BEFORE flowering by passing a 20-30 metre long coir or jute rope through the crop canopy. Pass the rope forward and then backward, both ways, while touching the crop canopy. Ensure water is standing in the crop during this operation. The rope dislodges and damages the larvae. After flowering, mechanical control no longer works - switch to chemical options. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I have rice plants showing dead hearts. What should I do?
output: Dead hearts (yellowing and drying of central shoot) indicate rice stem borer attack. Check what percentage of plants show the symptom. If more than 5 percent (the Economic Threshold Level), spray. Use 60 mL Coragen 18.5 SC, or 20 mL Fame 480 SC, or 50 g Takumi 20 WG, or 400 g Supremo 50 SP, or 170 g Mortar 75 SG, or 1 litre chlorpyriphos products, or 80 mL Ecotin (preferred at early stage) in 100 litres of water per acre. Repeat if damage reaches ETL again. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I see white-streaked folded leaves in my rice. What's wrong?
output: White streaks on folded rice leaves indicate leaf folder damage. The larvae fold leaves and eat the green tissue inside. The Economic Threshold Level is 10 percent leaf damage. Below ETL, monitor; at or above ETL, control with either mechanical (rope passing through canopy with standing water, before flowering only) or chemical control (60 mL Coragen 18.5 SC or alternatives in 100 litres water per acre). Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How does rope mechanical control of leaf folder work?
output: Use a 20-30 metre long coir or jute rope. Pass it across the rice crop canopy in both directions - forward then backward - while touching the canopy. Water must be standing in the crop during this operation. The rope dislodges and damages the leaf folder larvae hiding inside the folded leaves. This works only BEFORE flowering. After flowering, the canopy is too sensitive and chemical control is needed. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How is rice stem borer different from rice leaf folder?
output: Stem borer larvae bore INTO the stem - causing dead hearts (drying central shoot in young plants) or whiteheads (empty erect earheads in older plants). ETL: 5 percent dead hearts. Damage period: July to October. Leaf folder larvae fold the LEAVES and eat the green tissue from inside - leaving white streaks. ETL: 10 percent leaf damage. Damage period: August to October. Both respond to similar insecticides (Coragen, Fame, Takumi, etc.) but at different ETLs. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why does PAU recommend ETL-based spraying instead of routine sprays?
output: ETL-based spraying (Economic Threshold Level: 5 percent dead hearts for stem borer, 10 percent leaf damage for leaf folder, 5 planthoppers per hill for planthoppers) avoids unnecessary pesticide use. Below ETL, natural enemies and crop compensation handle the damage; spraying at sub-economic levels wastes money, kills beneficial insects, and accelerates pesticide resistance. ETL-based monitoring is the foundation of integrated pest management for rice. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What insecticides should I use for rice leaf folder at ETL?
output: When leaf damage reaches 10 percent (ETL), spray any of these in 100 litres of water per acre: 60 mL Coragen 18.5 SC (chlorantraniliprole), or 20 mL Fame 480 SC (flubendiamide 39.35%), or 50 g Takumi 20 WG (flubendiamide 20%), or 400 g Supremo 50 SP (thiocyclam hydrogen oxalate), or 170 g Mortar 75 SG (cartap hydrochloride), or 1 litre Coroban/Durmet/Force 20 EC (chlorpyriphos), or 80 mL Ecotin (azadirachtin 5%). Prefer Ecotin at pest initiation stage. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What are rice planthoppers and what damage do they cause?
output: Planthoppers include whitebacked planthopper (WBPH) and brown planthopper (BPH). Both nymphs and adults suck cell sap particularly from the leaf-sheath, from July to October. The crop dries up in patches. As plants die, hoppers migrate to adjacent plants and kill them too, expanding the dry patches over a few days. This is called hopper burn. Severe attack can destroy entire fields. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I monitor planthoppers in my rice field?
output: About one month after transplanting, slightly tilt a few plants and tap them 2 or 3 times at the base. Repeat at weekly intervals. Count planthoppers floating on the water around the tapped hills. The Economic Threshold Level (ETL) is a minimum of 5 planthoppers per hill. Spray when this level is reached. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the ETL for rice planthoppers?
output: The Economic Threshold Level for rice planthoppers is a minimum of 5 planthoppers per hill, observed by tilting and tapping plants and counting hoppers floating on water. Spray at or above this level. Below ETL, monitoring is sufficient - natural predators (spiders, mirid bugs, etc.) handle the population without intervention. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What insecticides can I use for rice planthoppers?
output: PAU lists 9 options at ETL (5 planthoppers per hill) in 100 litres of water per acre: 94 mL Pexalon 10 SC (triflumezopyrim), or 60 g Ulala 50 WG (flonicamid), or 80 g Osheen/Token/Dominant 20 SG (dinotefuran), or 120 g Chess 50 WG (pymetrozine), or 400 mL Orchestra 10 SC (benzpyrimoxan), or 300 mL Imagine/Viola 10 SC (flupyrimin), or 800 mL Ekalux/Quinguard/Quinalmass 25 EC (quinalphos), or 80 mL Ecotin (azadirachtin 5%), or 4 litres PAU Homemade Neem Extract. Prefer Ecotin or PAU Homemade Neem Extract at pest initiation stage. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is PAU Homemade Neem Extract for rice planthoppers?
output: PAU Homemade Neem Extract is a low-cost biological option for rice planthopper control. Apply 4 litres per acre in 100 litres of water. Prefer it at pest initiation stage along with Ecotin (azadirachtin 5%) before populations build up. The extract is prepared by farmers from neem leaves and is free or near-free, making it ideal for cost-conscious smallholders. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How should I spray for planthoppers to maximize effectiveness?
output: Use a knapsack sprayer and direct the spray towards the BASE of the plants - planthoppers feed at the base of rice stems and the leaf-sheath, so the spray must reach there. Top-down spraying misses the actual feeding zone. If damage is noticed at hopper-burn stage, treat the affected dry-patch spots PLUS a 3-4 metre periphery immediately because these spots harbour high insect populations. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I see dry patches in my rice field. What's wrong and what do I do?
output: Dry patches in rice are typical of planthopper hopper-burn damage. The hoppers feed at plant bases, kill plants in patches, and migrate outward expanding the patches. Treat the affected spots PLUS a 3-4 metre periphery immediately - the periphery harbours the high-density migrating populations. Use 94 mL Pexalon 10 SC, or 80 g Osheen, or any other recommended planthopper insecticide in 100 litres of water per acre, knapsack sprayer directed at plant bases. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I repeat spray for rice planthoppers after the first application?
output: Yes, repeat the spray if necessary - if planthopper populations rebuild to ETL (5 per hill) after the first spray. Continue ETL-based monitoring (weekly tap-count) and apply the next spray only when needed. Some seasons need two or three sprays; others need none. Avoid synthetic pyrethroids which trigger planthopper resurgence by killing predators. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is rice grasshopper damage and how do I control it?
output: Rice grasshoppers (adults and nymphs) eat leaves, especially in the nursery stage. The same insecticides recommended for planthopper control - Pexalon, Ulala, Osheen, Chess, Orchestra, Imagine, Ekalux, or biological options Ecotin and PAU Homemade Neem Extract - are also effective for grasshoppers. Monitor nursery and main crop, apply when damage is visible. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is rice hispa and where is it a problem?
output: Rice hispa is a serious pest in some areas of Gurdaspur and Amritsar districts, and is also found in other rice growing areas of Punjab. The grubs tunnel INTO the leaves while adults are exposed feeders on leaf surfaces. The grubs cause distinctive damage - bold, white streaks on the leaves. If unchecked, hispa can substantially reduce yield. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I see bold white streaks on my rice leaves. What is this damage?
output: Bold white streaks on rice leaves are characteristic of rice hispa damage. The grubs tunnel inside leaves, eating green tissue and leaving white windowpanes. This pest is especially serious in Gurdaspur and Amritsar districts. If the attack started in nursery, clip and destroy affected leaf tips before transplanting. On transplanted crop, spray 800 mL Ekalux 25 EC (quinalphos) or 1.0 litre Dursban 20 EC (chlorpyriphos) in 100 litres of water per acre with a manually operated sprayer. Repeat if attack persists. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I control rice hispa if I see attack in the nursery?
output: If rice hispa attack starts in the nursery, clip-off and destroy the leaf tips of the affected seedlings BEFORE transplanting. The grubs are inside the leaf tissue near the tips - removing this part eliminates the larval reservoir without needing chemical treatment in the nursery. Then transplant only clean seedlings to keep the main field free of the pest. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What insecticides work for rice hispa on transplanted crop?
output: On transplanted rice with hispa attack, spray either 800 mL Ekalux 25 EC (quinalphos) OR 1.0 litre Dursban 20 EC (chlorpyriphos) in 100 litres of water per acre with a manually operated sprayer. Repeat the spraying if the attack persists. The same insecticides are options in the planthopper control list, useful when both pests appear together. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is rice root weevil and where is it found?
output: Rice root weevil is a localized pest mainly in the rice-growing area around Rajpura. The white legless grubs feed on rice roots in the soil from July to September. Affected plants turn yellow, become stunted, and produce only a few tillers. The damage looks like nutrient deficiency at first but does not respond to fertilizer. Outside Rajpura, this pest is rarely a problem. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What does rice root weevil damage look like?
output: Rice plants attacked by root weevil show three symptoms: yellow leaves, stunted growth, and few tillers. The damage looks like nitrogen or other nutrient deficiency but does not improve with fertilizer because the white legless grubs are eating the roots in the soil. The damage period is July to September. The pest is localized to the Rajpura area in Punjab. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Summarize the Economic Threshold Levels for rice insect pests in Punjab.
output: PAU Economic Threshold Levels for need-based insecticide application: Stem borers - 5 percent dead hearts. Leaf folder - 10 percent leaf damage. Planthoppers - minimum 5 planthoppers per hill (counted by tilting and tapping plants weekly starting one month after transplanting). Spray only when damage reaches the ETL; below ETL, natural enemies and crop compensation handle the pressure. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the difference between whitebacked and brown planthopper?
output: Both species are rice planthoppers and PAU bundles them together for management. Whitebacked planthopper (WBPH, white stripe on back) is the carrier of Southern rice black-streaked dwarf virus (SRBSDV) - the rice dwarfing disease - making it especially serious. Brown planthopper (BPH, fully brown) is more directly damaging through hopper burn. Both nymphs and adults suck cell sap from leaf-sheaths. Same control measures apply to both: monitor at 5 per hill ETL, spray with Pexalon, Osheen, or other listed options. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is rice ear-cutting caterpillar (armyworm) damage?
output: Rice ear-cutting caterpillar - commonly called armyworm - is gregarious. Young larvae feed on leaves leaving only the mid-ribs and stems. Old larvae cut off panicles mostly at the base, which is how the pest gets its name. This stage causes serious yield loss because cut panicles cannot recover. The larvae are shy of sunlight and feed mainly at night. Damage period: September to November. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When does rice armyworm cause damage?
output: Rice ear-cutting caterpillar (armyworm) damage occurs mainly from September to November - during the panicle development and grain-fill stages. Young larvae eat leaves leaving only mid-ribs and stems. Old larvae cut entire panicles at the base. The larvae feed at night and hide during the day. Late-season vigilance is essential because the timing coincides with the most yield-determining stages. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is rice dwarfing disease?
output: Rice dwarfing disease is caused by Southern rice black-streaked dwarf virus (SRBSDV). It is a newly emerging viral disease in Punjab, and ALL PAU-recommended rice varieties are susceptible. Infected plants are severely stunted, may stay only one-third to two-thirds of normal height. Leaves become short, dark green, and stiff. Roots remain shallow so plants can be easily uprooted. Affected plants wither, have poor panicle emergence, and produce mostly unfilled grains - causing heavy yield loss. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What does rice dwarfing disease look like?
output: Rice dwarfing disease (SRBSDV viral disease) shows severe stunting - plants stay only one-third to two-thirds of normal height. Leaves are short, dark green, and stiff. Roots remain shallow making plants easy to uproot. Plants do not respond to fertilizer (unlike nutrient deficiency). Affected plants wither, panicles emerge poorly, and grains are mostly unfilled - resulting in heavy yield loss. The virus is transmitted by whitebacked planthopper. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How does rice dwarfing disease spread?
output: Rice dwarfing disease (SRBSDV) is transmitted by the whitebacked planthopper (WBPH). The virus has no curative treatment - management is preventive. Three steps: (1) Maintain bunds and irrigation channels free from weeds (which host the vector). (2) Inspect crop regularly for stunted plants; promptly remove and deep-bury infected plants. (3) Continuously monitor both nursery and transplanted fields for WBPH; apply recommended planthopper insecticides if WBPH is observed. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I manage rice dwarfing disease in my field?
output: Since there is no curative treatment for the virus, focus on prevention: (1) Keep bunds and irrigation channels free of weeds that host the whitebacked planthopper vector. (2) Walk the field regularly and watch for stunted plants - remove and deep-bury infected plants promptly to stop the source. (3) Monitor for whitebacked planthopper in nursery and main field; spray recommended planthopper insecticides if observed. ALL PAU rice varieties are susceptible, so no resistant variety option exists. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I see greyish green lesions with purple margins on rice leaf-sheath. What's wrong?
output: Greyish green lesions with purple margin on rice leaf-sheath above the water level are classic sheath blight - a fungal disease caused by Rhizoctonia solani. Lesions enlarge and coalesce. Severe attack causes poor grain filling. To manage: spray as soon as the disease appears (maximum tillering to boot stage) with one of the recommended fungicides like Ayaan 48 WG (200 g per acre) or Tilt 25 EC (200 mL per acre) in 200 litres of water. Give second spray 15 days later. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How can I prevent rice sheath blight without spraying?
output: Three cultural measures: (1) Destroy rice straw and stubbles after harvesting an affected crop - this removes the inoculum source for next season. (2) Avoid excessive use of nitrogenous fertilizers - lush canopies favour the disease. (3) Keep bunds clean by removing grass, which can host the fungus. Combine with PAU-LCC for need-based nitrogen, and the disease pressure stays low without fungicide. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I spray fungicide for rice sheath blight?
output: Spray as soon as the disease appears, between maximum tillering and boot stage of the crop. Earlier is wasted; later misses the protective window because the lesions have already girdled the stems. Use 200 g Ayaan 48 WG, OR 600 g Avancer Glow 75 WG, OR 150 mL Iglare/Pulsor 24 SC, OR 200 mL Tilt/Bumper/Pikapika 25 EC, OR 80 g Nativo 75 WG, OR 200 mL Monceren 250 SC, etc., in 200 litres of water per acre. Give a second spray 15 days later. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What fungicides can I use for rice sheath blight?
output: PAU lists 10 options at maximum tillering to boot stage in 200 litres of water per acre: 200 g Ayaan 48 WG (kresoxim methyl + hexaconazole), or 600 g Avancer Glow 75 WG (azoxystrobin + mancozeb), or 150 mL Iglare/Pulsor 24 SC (thifluzamide), or 26.8 g Epic 75 WG (hexaconazole), or 400 mL Galileo Way 18.76 SC, or 200 mL Amistar Top 325 SC, or 200 mL Tilt/Bumper/Pikapika 25 EC (propiconazole), or 200 mL Folicur/Orius 25 EC (tebuconazole), or 80 g Nativo 75 WG (trifloxystrobin + tebuconazole), or 320 mL Lusture 37.5 SE (flusilazole + carbendazim), or 200 mL Monceren 250 SC (pencycuron). Give second spray 15 days later. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why does PAU say not to use excess nitrogen if I want to avoid sheath blight?
output: Excessive nitrogen creates dense lush canopies that favour the Rhizoctonia solani fungus that causes sheath blight. The thick canopy retains humidity at the leaf-sheath level and makes plants more susceptible. Use PAU-LCC for need-based urea application instead of fixed doses, especially around the maximum tillering stage when sheath blight risk is highest. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What active ingredients are in Ayaan 48 WG fungicide?
output: Ayaan 48 WG is a combination fungicide containing kresoxim methyl 40 percent plus hexaconazole 8 percent. Apply 200 g per acre in 200 litres of water for rice sheath blight at maximum tillering to boot stage. The combination of two active ingredients with different modes of action improves efficacy and slows resistance development. Give a second spray 15 days later. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I use Avancer Glow for rice sheath blight?
output: Avancer Glow 75 WG contains azoxystrobin 8.3 percent plus mancozeb 66.7 percent. Apply 600 g per acre in 200 litres of water for rice sheath blight, starting at maximum tillering to boot stage when the disease appears. Give a second spray 15 days later. The combination of strobilurin (azoxystrobin) plus contact (mancozeb) gives both systemic and protective action. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is Tilt for rice sheath blight and how do I apply it?
output: Tilt 25 EC (also sold as Bumper, Pikapika) contains propiconazole - a triazole systemic fungicide. Apply 200 mL per acre in 200 litres of water for rice sheath blight at maximum tillering to boot stage. Give a second spray 15 days later. Tilt has been a long-standing standard for sheath blight control in Punjab rice. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is Nativo and what does it control in rice?
output: Nativo 75 WG is a combination fungicide containing trifloxystrobin plus tebuconazole. Apply 80 g per acre in 200 litres of water for rice sheath blight at maximum tillering to boot stage. Give a second spray 15 days later. The strobilurin plus triazole combination provides both protective and curative action against Rhizoctonia solani. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Should I always give a second spray for rice sheath blight?
output: Yes - PAU's standard recommendation is to give a second spray 15 days after the first for ALL listed sheath blight fungicides. The first spray protects existing tissue; the second spray covers new growth and any infections that established between sprays. The 15-day interval matches the residual activity of the fungicides and the time for the disease to re-establish if untreated. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Summarize PAU's rice diseases and key controls.
output: Three major rice diseases in PAU's Punjab program. (1) Rice dwarfing disease (SRBSDV virus) - all varieties susceptible, no curative treatment, prevent via weed-free bunds and removing infected plants and controlling whitebacked planthopper vector. (2) Sheath blight (Rhizoctonia solani fungus) - greyish lesions with purple margin on leaf-sheath; spray Ayaan, Avancer Glow, Tilt, Nativo, etc. at maximum tillering to boot stage, second spray 15 days later. (3) False smut - spray fungicides at boot stage to prevent. Plus avoid excess nitrogen and synthetic pyrethroids which trigger pest cascades. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is rice false smut and what causes it?
output: False smut is a fungal disease of rice caused by Ustilaginoidea virens. Individual grains transform into large yellowish or greenish velvety spore-balls. High relative humidity, rainy and cloudy days during flowering, plus high doses of nitrogenous fertilizers and excessive organic manures all increase disease intensity. Spray fungicide preventively at boot stage in disease-prone areas. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I see large yellowish or greenish velvety balls instead of grains in my rice. What is this?
output: This is false smut, caused by the fungus Ustilaginoidea virens. Individual rice grains transform into yellowish or greenish velvety spore-balls. The disease is favoured by humid, rainy, cloudy weather during flowering, and is worsened by excessive nitrogen or organic manure application. Once visible, control is difficult - prevent next season by spraying recommended fungicide at boot stage in disease-prone areas, and avoid excessive nitrogen. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I prevent rice false smut?
output: Spray preventively at boot stage in disease-prone areas with either 400 mL Galileo Way 18.76 SC (picoxystrobin plus propiconazole) per acre OR 500 g Kocide 46 DF (copper hydroxide) per acre, in 200 litres of water. Boot stage is when the panicle is fully formed inside the flag leaf sheath, just before emergence - the moment of vulnerability. Also avoid excessive nitrogen and excessive organic manures, both of which worsen the disease. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I spray for rice false smut?
output: Spray at the BOOT stage of the rice crop, before the panicle emerges from the flag leaf sheath. This is the preventive window - once the panicle has emerged and grains have transformed into velvety spore-balls, no fungicide will reverse the damage. Use 400 mL Galileo Way 18.76 SC or 500 g Kocide 46 DF per acre in 200 litres of water. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is rice brown leaf spot?
output: Brown leaf spot is caused by the fungus Drechslera oryzae. It produces oval eye-shaped spots with a conspicuous dark-brown dot in the centre and light brown margin. Spots also develop on the grains. The disease occurs in poor soils, so give adequate and balanced nutrition to the crop. Spray two times with 80 g Nativo 75 WG (trifloxystrobin plus tebuconazole) in 200 litres of water per acre - first at boot stage, second 15 days later. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I see oval eye-shaped brown spots on my rice leaves. What is this?
output: Oval, eye-shaped spots with a conspicuous dark-brown dot in the centre and light-brown margin are characteristic brown leaf spot, caused by Drechslera oryzae. Spots also appear on grains. This disease indicates poor soil nutrition - the crop is stressed and susceptible. Correct the nutrition and spray 80 g Nativo 75 WG per acre in 200 litres of water at boot stage and again 15 days later. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is rice blast disease?
output: Rice blast is a serious fungal disease caused by Pyricularia grisea. It produces spindle-shaped spots with greyish centre and brown margin on leaves at maximum tillering. It also causes brown lesions on the neck of the panicle (neck rot), making panicles fall over. The disease is more severe on Basmati cultivars in sub-montaneous areas and under heavy nitrogen application. Spray 200 mL Amistar Top 325 SC or 500 g Indofil Z-78 75 WP per acre in 200 litres of water at boot and ear-emergence stages. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I see spindle-shaped greyish spots with brown margin on rice leaves. What's wrong?
output: These are classic symptoms of rice blast (Pyricularia grisea fungus) at maximum tillering. The disease can progress to neck rot - brown lesions on the panicle neck causing panicles to fall over. More severe on Basmati cultivars, sub-montaneous areas, and fields with heavy nitrogen. Spray 200 mL Amistar Top 325 SC (azoxystrobin plus difenoconazole) per acre OR 500 g Indofil Z-78 75 WP (zineb) per acre in 200 litres of water, at boot stage and ear-emergence stages. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why is rice blast more severe on Basmati varieties in sub-montaneous Punjab?
output: Basmati cultivars are more susceptible to Pyricularia grisea than non-Basmati PR varieties, especially in sub-montaneous areas where higher humidity and cooler nights favour the fungus. Heavy nitrogen application worsens susceptibility further by producing lush canopies. PAU recommends spraying 200 mL Amistar Top or 500 g Indofil Z-78 per acre at boot stage and ear-emergence stages, plus avoiding excessive nitrogen on Basmati in sub-montaneous areas. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: When should I spray for rice blast?
output: Spray at boot stage and again at ear-emergence stage. Two sprays are needed because the disease can progress from leaf blast at maximum tillering to the more damaging neck rot at panicle emergence. Use 200 mL Amistar Top 325 SC (azoxystrobin plus difenoconazole) or 500 g Indofil Z-78 75 WP (zineb) per acre in 200 litres of water. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What conditions favour rice diseases in Punjab?
output: PAU lists these as favourable for disease development: early transplanting, excessive ponding of water, continuous drizzling, 25-30 degrees Celsius temperature, high relative humidity, and excessive use of nitrogen. Avoid these by transplanting in the recommended window (20 June to 10 July), draining and intermittent irrigation after the 2-week establishment period, and using PAU-LCC for need-based nitrogen. Monitor regularly for sheath blight especially. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is the general PAU advice for preventing rice diseases?
output: Three principles. (1) Avoid excessive use of nitrogen - lush canopies favour sheath blight, false smut, blast, and other diseases. (2) Monitor the crop regularly for sheath blight appearance and apply recommended fungicides timely. (3) For false smut management, apply PREVENTIVE fungicide spray at boot stage - waiting until symptoms show is too late. Plus avoid early transplanting, excessive ponding, and use PAU-LCC for need-based urea. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is rice bunt or kernel smut?
output: Bunt or Kernel Smut is a fungal disease of rice caused by Neovossia horrida. Only a few grains in the panicle are infected - frequently only a part of the grain is replaced by black powder. Sometimes the entire grain is attacked and the black powder scatters onto other grains or leaves, which is often how farmers first notice the disease. Avoid heavy doses of nitrogenous fertilizers to reduce risk. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I see black powder on some of my rice grains. What is this?
output: Black powder on rice grains is the typical sign of bunt (also called kernel smut), caused by Neovossia horrida. Frequently only part of the grain is replaced by black powder; sometimes the entire grain is filled. The black spores scatter onto other grains and leaves - that scattering is often the easiest way to detect the disease in the field. Avoid heavy nitrogen application to reduce next-season risk. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is rice sheath rot?
output: Sheath rot is caused by the fungus Fusarium moniliforme. The rot occurs on the uppermost leaf-sheaths where oblong to irregular grey-brown to light-brown lesions develop. Lesions coalesce to cover the entire sheath. In severe cases, young panicles either do not emerge or emerge only partially. A white powdery fungal growth appears on the panicle inside the sheath. Glumes of infected florets are discoloured (dark-red, purple-brown, or black) and often do not fill. The fungus overwinters in rice straw and grains - destroy infected residue to break the cycle. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: My rice panicles do not emerge fully. Could it be sheath rot?
output: Possibly. Severe sheath rot (Fusarium moniliforme) prevents young panicles from emerging or makes them emerge only partially. Look for oblong grey-brown to light-brown lesions on the uppermost leaf-sheaths that coalesce to cover the whole sheath, plus a white powdery fungal growth on the panicle inside the sheath. Glumes of any emerged florets will be discoloured (dark red, purple-brown, or black) and often unfilled. Destroy infected straw and grains to remove the overwintering fungus. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Why does PAU recommend destroying rice residue from disease-affected fields?
output: Many rice fungi - Rhizoctonia solani (sheath blight), Fusarium moniliforme (sheath rot), Drechslera oryzae (brown leaf spot), and others - overwinter in rice straw and grain debris. If you leave infected residue in the field, the fungus survives and infects next year's crop, even if you switch varieties. Destroy infected straw to break the disease cycle. This conflicts with paddy straw retention practices, so destruction is reserved for fields with confirmed disease. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: Compare rice false smut and rice blast - which is worse and where?
output: Both are serious but affect different areas. False smut (Ustilaginoidea virens) - grains turn into yellowish/greenish velvety spore-balls; favoured by humid rainy cloudy weather during flowering and excess nitrogen; manage by preventive boot-stage spray of 400 mL Galileo Way or 500 g Kocide. Blast (Pyricularia grisea) - spindle spots on leaves and neck-rot lesions; more severe on Basmati cultivars in sub-montaneous areas with heavy nitrogen; manage by 200 mL Amistar Top or 500 g Indofil Z-78 at boot AND ear-emergence stages. Both worsened by excess nitrogen, both prevented by need-based PAU-LCC nitrogen approach. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: How do I control rice sheath rot?
output: For rice sheath rot (Fusarium moniliforme), three steps: (1) Destroy the rice straw after harvesting the infected crop because the fungus overwinters there. (2) Use disease-free seed for next sowing. (3) Give two sprays of 26.8 g Epic 75 WG (hexaconazole) in 200 litres of water per acre - first at boot stage, second 15 days afterwards. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is rice stem rot?
output: Rice stem rot is caused by Sclerotium oryzae fungus. It affects the stem at earing stage. Black lesions develop on the sheath at the water level. Later the stem gets infected and rots, causing withering and lodging of plants. Incidence has declined on high-yielding varieties due to improved cultural practices. Destroy diseased debris, avoid excessive irrigation, and use only the recommended dose of nitrogenous fertilizer. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I see black lesions on my rice sheath at water level and the plants are lodging. What's wrong?
output: This pattern - black lesions on sheath at water level, then stem rot and lodging - indicates rice stem rot caused by Sclerotium oryzae. The fungus enters at the water-line and rots the stem, weakening it until it falls. Manage by destroying infected crop debris, avoiding excessive irrigation, and using only the recommended nitrogen dose (excess N worsens the disease). Modern PAU rice varieties have reduced this disease's prevalence. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: What is bacterial blight in rice?
output: Bacterial blight is caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae. Greenish-yellow stripes appear along leaf margins, extending both lengthwise and breadthwise. The leaf starts drying from the tip, becomes white in severe cases, and dries completely. The disease can attack freshly transplanted seedlings, causing wilting and full clump death within days. The bacterium overwinters in seed, rice straw, and roots of non-host plants. Source: PAU Package of Practices Kharif 2025.

instruction: I see greenish-yellow stripes along my rice leaf margins. What is this?
output: Greenish-yellow stripes along leaf margins extending lengthwise and breadthwise are classic bacterial blight (Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae). Leaves start drying from the tip and turn white in severe cases. The bacterium overwinters in seed, straw, and weed roots.
